title: Microenvironmental barriers to healing in osteoradionecrosis and opportunities for regenerative intervention.
authors: Aleyna E La Croix; Maria Eduarda Torres Gouveia; Peter M Bertone; Neva M Nemanic; Chelsea S Bahney; Katherine R Hixon
abstract: Osteoradionecrosis (ORN) is a debilitating sequela of radiotherapy (RT) for head and neck cancer (HNC), characterized by persistent bone exposure or radiographic non-viability and profound tissue repair failure. Despite advances in radiation delivery and clinical management, ORN remains challenging to treat, with therapeutic strategies largely focused on symptom control, infection mitigation, or surgical reconstruction rather than restoration of regenerative capacity. Emerging evidence suggests that radiation-induced cellular senescence represents a central and underrecognized driver of ORN pathophysiology. Ionizing radiation disrupts the bone microenvironment through sustained vascular injury, impaired osteogenic-angiogenic coupling, chronic inflammation, and the accumulation of senescent bone-resident and stromal cells that secrete a pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Together, these changes create a hostile niche that suppresses bone remodeling and wound healing long after radiation exposure. This review synthesizes current understanding of radiation-induced injury to the bone microenvironment, critically evaluates existing classification systems and treatment strategies for ORN, and examines emerging regenerative approaches. We further propose senotherapeutic strategies targeting radiation-induced cellular senescence as a complementary and potentially transformative avenue to restore tissue repair capacity. By integrating regenerative biomaterials with targeted modulation of senescence, future therapies may move beyond palliation toward true biological resolution of ORN. Biomaterial delivery systems (e.g., injectable hydrogels, mineral composite scaffolds, and cryogel platforms) are emerging as promising vehicles for spatiotemporally controlled senotherapeutic delivery within the irradiated bone niche.

title: Triple-pathway synergistic senolysis via AKAP1 silencing and calcium overload: An aptamer-functionalized DNAzyme nanoplatform for anti-pulmonary fibrosis research.
authors: Jianqiong Pan; Liuqin Teng; Jiaqiong Wu; Xiao Li; Dongdong Zhang; Qingao Meng; Chengkai Zhuang; Ting Chen; Xiahui Lin; Shanni Hong
abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) lacks therapies that reverse disease progression, partly due to persistent senescent alveolar epithelial type II cells (SAEC II). We report a synergistic senolytic strategy combining mitochondrial calcium overload with AKAP1 silencing. An acid-responsive nanoplatform (CCMD@Lipo-Apt) comprising a CaCO3 core co-loaded with curcumin (CUR), Mn2+, and an AKAP1-targeting DNAzyme, enveloped by an L1CAM aptamer-modified lipid bilayer, enables SAEC II-specific homing. Upon lysosomal acidification, CaCO3 degrades to release Ca2+, CUR (mobilizing ER Ca2+), Mn2+, and the DNAzyme. Mn2+ simultaneously activates DNAzyme to knockdown AKAP1 (sensitizing mitochondria to calcium overload) and directly activates caspase-8. This triple mechanism collapses mitochondrial membrane potential and triggers robust apoptosis exclusively in SAEC II. In a bleomycin-induced mouse model, CCMD@Lipo-Apt clears SAEC II, attenuates fibrosis, and restores lung function without overt toxicity. This work establishes a synthetic-lethal axis for targeted IPF therapy.

title: From protection to progression: How CCT/TRiC shapes therapy-induced senescence in glioblastoma multiforme.
journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular basis of disease
authors: Maria Antonella Augello; Maciej Wnuk; Celeste Caruso Bavisotto; Francesco Cappello; Federica Scalia
abstract: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most lethal primary brain tumor despite maximal resection, radiotherapy, and temozolomide. Growing evidence indicates that standard therapies drive many GBM cells into therapy-induced senescence (TIS), marked by permanent proliferation arrest, high metabolic activity, and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Although senescent cells may initially limit growth, their persistence can fuel recurrence by altering the microenvironment while driving immunosuppression and stem-like traits. GBM is also "chaperone dependent," relying on proteostasis networks for rapid growth, invasion, and treatment resistance. The eukaryotic chaperonin CCT/TRiC, an ATP-dependent complex of eight subunits (CCT1-CCT8), is essential for folding actin and tubulin and for the maturation of multiple oncogenic clients. We review recent findings on CCT/TRiC subunit dysregulation in GBM and propose a mechanistic link between chaperonin activity and senescence, integrating p53/p21 and p16INK4a/Rb signaling, EGFR-driven survival, hypoxia/HIF-mediated metabolic reprogramming, and immune infiltration in high-SASP tumors. We discuss how CCT/TRiC is probably involved in maintaining glioma stem cell (GSC) proteostasis by modulating EGFR, TGF-β, mTOR, Wnt/β-catenin, and Notch pathways, thereby supporting GSC survival, self-renewal, and invasiveness. We also propose how CCT/TRiC inhibition can lead to impaired macroautophagy by disrupting mTOR signaling-both crucial for sustaining senescence and SASP-thereby compromising proteostasis and autophagic flux. Finally, we outline possible therapeutic strategies based on this axis, including novel combinations of senolytics, immunotherapy potentiators, and CCT/TRiC-targeted agents to prevent SASP-driven progression and relapse.

title: Innovative niosome screening for efficient gene delivery in senescent primary umbilical cord stroma-derived MSCs.
authors: Alba Iglesias-Fente; Junquera López-Seijas; María C Arufe; Juan Antonio Fafián-Labora; Ana Rey-Rico
abstract: The potential of senescent cell clearance to extend healthspan and delay the onset of age-related diseases has driven the development of innovative senotherapeutics. Thus, niosome-based gene therapy has emerged as a promising strategy to overcome the off-target limitations of first-generation senolytics, senomorphics, and senoreverts. In the present study, we investigated two new niosome formulations for genetically modifying primary umbilical cord stroma senescent MSCs (UC-MSCs) in a Palbociclib-induced senescent model, using non-senescent UC-MSCs as a control. These niosomes were formulated by fixing the cationic lipid composition (1,2-di-O-octadecenyl-3 trimethylammonium propane, DOTMA, D) and varying the non-ionic surfactants (polysorbate 20, P20, or polysorbate 80, P80) and the helper lipids (chloroquine, CQ, or cholesterol, CH) (DP20CQ and DP80CH, respectively) at two mole ratios (1:2:1 and 1:2:2 for DP20CQ; 1:2:2 and 1:2:4 for DP80CH). Results on transfection revealed that the DP20CQ formulations outperformed those with DP80CH in both UC-MSCs phenotypes from four different donors. Notably, DP20CQ niosomes prepared at 10/1 and 15/1 DOTMA/DNA ratios achieved the highest transgene expression levels in senescent UC-MSCs, surpassing even the commercial reagent Lipofectamine. Further, DP20CQ formulations exhibited adequate physicochemical properties for transfection and promoted a marked endosomal escape, particularly at the DOTMA/DNA ratio 10/1, without compromising cell viability. These findings underscore the value of niosomes as robust gene delivery vehicles for senescent cells in therapeutic antiaging strategies.

title: The role of immune aging in rheumatoid arthritis and its clinical and therapeutic significance.
authors: Yong Wei; WenXia Qi; Pingshun Li; Tao Wang; Zhandong Wang; Hailong Liu; Yuanyuan Zhang; Jiexiang Tian; Gang Wang
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease, and its onset and progression are closely related to age-related remodeling of the immune system. Immunosenescence refers to age-related changes in the overall structure and function of the immune system; inflammaging is a persistent, low-grade, systemic inflammatory state; cellular senescence refers to a relatively stable cell cycle arrest and functional remodeling of cells under continuous stress. These three are interrelated but correspond to the immune system, systemic inflammatory environment, and cellular state, respectively; therefore, they should not be used interchangeably. In RA, especially elderly-onset RA (EORA), immune age-related changes may occur earlier or be more severe. Human studies on RA mainly support that immune cell lineage remodeling, senescence-associated cell phenotypes, and changes in inflammatory mediators are associated with disease activity, structural damage, and some extra-articular comorbidities. Immunosenescence may compromise T-cell, B-cell, and innate immune functions; concurrently, local cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) may drive synovial and bone marrow microenvironment remodeling, while inflammaging may further amplify systemic inflammation. Impaired immune clearance, accumulation of senescent cells, and SASP release may establish a self-perpetuating cycle and are associated with autoantibody production, bone loss, cartilage damage, and cardiovascular and neuropsychiatric comorbidities. However, causal evidence for SASP-driven RA synovitis and the efficacy of senolytic interventions is still primarily derived from experimental arthritis, osteoarthritis, and other non-RA disease models. This article clarifies the definitions and delineates the applicable boundaries of these three terms, reviews their systemic phenotypes, cell lineage characteristics, and molecular basis in RA, especially EORA, analyzes the links between immune age and disease activity, autoantibodies, synovial microenvironment, bone and cartilage damage, and extra-articular manifestations, and evaluates the potential benefits, risks, and evidence limitations of traditional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), biologic agents, and emerging senescence-targeting strategies. By constructing an integrated framework covering immune system remodeling, local cellular senescence, inflammatory amplification, and clinical outcomes, this article aims to provide a theoretical basis for further research on EORA risk stratification and immunosenescence-related interventions, rather than directly translating unverified mechanisms into clinical conclusions.

title: Stem cell senescence as a regenerative bottleneck in age-related skeletal degeneration: Mechanistic crosstalk and translational strategies.
authors: Xinling Wang; Yong Huang; Tianming Zhu; Heng Qiu
abstract: Skeletal degeneration is a major cause of pain, disability, fragility fracture, and loss of independence in aging populations. Although osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration are usually managed as anatomically separate disorders, they share a common regenerative failure: endogenous stem and progenitor cells lose renewal capacity, acquire inflammatory secretory programs, and become less able to rebuild damaged matrix. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on senescence in bone marrow mesenchymal stem/stromal cells, skeletal stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells, cartilage progenitor cells, synovial mesenchymal stromal cells, and disc-derived progenitor populations. Priority is given to primary mechanistic, omics, translational, and early clinical studies that connect senescence markers with functional impairment or intervention response. We discuss telomere-associated DNA damage, mitochondrial and oxidative stress, nutrient- and mechanosensing pathways, epigenetic remodeling, dysregulated autophagy and mitophagy, and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype as interlocking mechanisms that reshape skeletal niches. Disease-specific sections then examine how senescent progenitor compartments drive osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and intervertebral disc degeneration through impaired osteogenesis or chondrogenesis, matrix catabolism, inflammatory vesicle signaling, and maladaptive mechanical feedback. Finally, we compare senolytics, senomorphics, metabolic and mitochondrial regulators, cell rejuvenation, extracellular vesicle engineering, biomaterials, and gene-based delivery platforms from a regenerative medicine perspective. Stem/progenitor cell senescence should be treated not simply as a biomarker of aging, but as a compartment-specific therapeutic bottleneck. Translation will require rigorous cell identity, multi-parameter senescence assays, disease-stage stratification, and therapies that restore regenerative competence without suppressing physiological repair.

title: Artificial intelligence and in silico discovery of senolytic and senescence-associated food peptides.
authors: Chi-Ching Lee; Itthanan Suttikhana; Tolulope Joshua Ashaolu
abstract: Cellular senescence, characterized by the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, is a primary driver of age-related tissue dysfunction. While synthetic senolytics have shown promise, concerns regarding systemic toxicity have shifted focus toward sustainable alternatives like food-derived bioactive peptides. This review evaluates AI and in silico methods in senolytic food peptide research, distinguishing discovery, prioritization, and unverified senescence relevance. We evaluate discovery pipelines across soy, dairy, legumes, and marine sources, addressing pharmacokinetics, bioavailability, senescence heterogeneity, gastrointestinal stability, bitterness, and the lack of standardized replicative and therapy-induced experimental senescence models. We further highlight that a substantial proportion of peptides discussed in the current literature are best characterized as senescence-associated candidates that await mechanistic validation, rather than as confirmed senolytics or senomorphics. Future research must prioritize bioengineered 3D human tissue models and long-term clinical validation.

title: Berberine as a multi-hallmark modulator of aging: From AMPK and mitophagy to inflammaging and the SASP.
authors: Sultan Mohammed Alanazi; Hayder M Al-Kuraishy; Ahmed M Abdelaziz; Eidah M Alasmari; Fatimah M Yousef; Ahmed A Mohamed; Mohamed M Salama; Gaber El-Saber Batiha
abstract: Berberine, a naturally occurring isoquinoline alkaloid found in several medicinal plants such as Berberis spp. and Coptis chinensis has long been used in traditional medicine. Recent evidence positions berberine as a pleiotropic modulator of multiple interconnected hallmarks of aging, making it a promising candidate for geroprotective interventions. This review critically examines the molecular mechanisms through which berberine influences energy metabolism, mitochondrial homeostasis, proteostasis, chronic inflammation, and cellular senescence. Berberine activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) via mild mitochondrial complex I inhibition, restoring cellular energy balance and suppressing mTOR-dependent anabolic pathways. Enhanced AMPK signaling stimulates autophagic flux and mitophagy, promoting clearance of damaged mitochondria and aggregated proteins. At the mitochondrial level, berberine improves respiratory efficiency, limits pathological excessive reactive oxygen species production while preserving physiological redox signaling, and upregulates endogenous antioxidant defenses through Nrf2. Furthermore, berberine exerts anti-inflammatory effects by inhibiting NF-κB nuclear translocation and reducing the transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β). Notably, berberine acts as a senomorphic agent, attenuating the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) without inducing widespread apoptosis, partly through modulation of p16 and cyclin expression. By integrating these molecular insights, this review positions berberine as a multi-target geromodulator that addresses deregulated nutrient sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired proteostasis, chronic inflammation, and cellular senescence in a coordinated manner. The translational potential, pharmacokinetic challenges, and safety considerations of berberine in the context of healthy aging are also discussed.

title: Nutrient-Sensitive Senescence Checkpoints in Diabetic Kidney Disease.
authors: Rui Ji; Qian Yang; Hongtu Hu
abstract: UNLABELLED: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) remains a leading cause of chronic kidney disease and kidney failure despite advances in glucose-lowering, hemodynamic, anti-inflammatory, and cardiorenal protective therapies. Cellular senescence has emerged as a key cell fate pathway linking persistent diabetic stress to renal inflammation, fibrosis, impaired repair, and progressive nephron loss. However, senescence in DKD should not be viewed simply as a terminal response to hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, or DNA damage. In this article, we define nutrient-sensitive senescence checkpoints as metabolic decision nodes that integrate amino acid flux, mitochondrial quality control, lipid routing, redox balance, oxygen stress, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) proteostasis, and inflammatory danger signaling to determine renal cell fate. We distinguish classical senescence in proliferative renal cells from senescence-like dysfunction in postmitotic podocytes, and we emphasize that interpretation requires a composite phenotype rather than any single marker. We discuss how serine, branched chain amino acids, arginine-citrulline metabolism, tryptophan-derived metabolites, and carnitine-linked lipid handling shape cell fate pathways in podocytes, tubular epithelial cells, endothelial cells, and immune-stromal compartments. We further examine how mitophagy, ferroptotic lipid peroxidation, ER stress, mitochondrial DNA leakage, cGAS-STING activation, AMPK-mTOR signaling, NAD+-sirtuin pathways, and nuclear receptor networks convert nutrient stress into maladaptive renal aging. Finally, we outline therapeutic opportunities to reprogram nutrient-sensitive senescence, including established DKD therapies, mitochondrial quality control enhancement, lipid-routing correction, senolytics, senomorphics, hypoxia-inducible factor pathway modulation, and biomarker-guided precision medicine. ARTICLE HIGHLIGHTS: Diabetic kidney disease remains progressive in many patients despite modern cardiorenal therapies, suggesting that additional persistent cell fate pathways sustain kidney injury. An unresolved question is how nutrient-derived signals determine whether renal cells undergo adaptive repair or maladaptive senescence-like dysfunction. Amino acid flux, mitophagy, lipid routing, redox balance, endoplasmic reticulum proteostasis, and inflammatory danger signaling may form nutrient-sensitive senescence checkpoints in diabetic kidney disease. Distinguishing cell cycle arrest in proliferative cells from composite senescence-like injury in postmitotic cells may improve biomarker-based patient stratification and guide metabolism-informed senescence-targeted therapies.

title: Cellular Senescence in Diabetic Cardiomyopathy: Mechanistic Insights and Therapeutic Perspectives.
authors: Ting Ye; Donglin Yang; Xinrui Chang; Dongdong Wu; Yuman Lei; Chengcheng Mu; Yizhe Zhao; Shouzhu Xu
abstract: Diabetic cardiomyopathyis a distinct cardiac disorder marked by diabetes-associated myocardial structural and functional abnormalities, developing independently of other overt cardiovascular diseases. Mounting evidence suggests that cellularsenescence serves as a central mechanism, linking metabolic stress to mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and adverse cardiac remodeling. In the diabetic heart, senescence manifests as sustained cell-cycle arrest, impaired mitochondrial function, and a proinflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). These features collectively drive detrimental structural and functional remodeling. Mechanistically, this process involves defective mitochondrial quality control, influenced by regulators such as Sirtuin 3 (SIRT3) and ATP synthase O subunit (ATP5O). Furthermore, aberrant activation of signaling pathways, including p53, FOXO1-Angiopoietin-like 4 (ANGPTL4), and various miRNA-dependent mechanisms, drives senescence in both cardiomyocytes and cardiac progenitor cells under diabetic conditions. Epigenetic remodeling and RNA methylation further shape this process by influencing transcriptional regulation and proteostasis. Concurrently, immunoinflammatory crosstalk, particularly macrophage polarization and persistent SASP-mediated inflammation, exacerbates myocardial fibrosis and dysfunction. It is notable that type 1 and type 2 diabetes present distinct patterns of senescence burden, mitochondrial impairment, and cardiac phenotypes.Promising therapeutic strategies targeting senescence-associated pathways, including senolytics, metabolic modulators, mitochondrial protectants, and epigenetic regulators, have demonstrated potential in preclinical and emerging clinical studies. This review integrates current insights into the complex interplay among metabolic stress, mitochondrial injury, and cellular senescence in Diabetic cardiomyopathy. It also highlights promising directions for mechanism-based interventions aimed at combating diabetic cardiac remodeling.

title: Cellular senescence in kidney diseases: a bibliometric analysis of global trends, knowledge bases, and emerging therapeutic frontiers.
authors: Ning Liu; Tao Liu
abstract: PURPOSE: Cellular senescence has emerged as an important mechanism linking renal ageing, acute kidney injury, diabetic kidney disease, chronic kidney disease, renal fibrosis, and kidney transplantation-related injury. This study aimed to map the global research landscape, knowledge bases, and emerging frontiers of cellular senescence-related kidney disease research. METHODS: Publications were retrieved from the Science Citation Index Expanded of the Web of Science Core Collection. After screening by language and document type, 775 English-language articles and reviews were included. CiteSpace and VOSviewer were used to analyze publication trends, citation impact, collaboration networks, productive countries, institutions, authors, journals, highly cited documents, co-cited references, keyword co-occurrence, and citation bursts. RESULTS: The field expanded rapidly after 2016 and reached its highest annual output in 2025. China and the United States were the leading contributors by publication volume. Co-cited reference clustering identified major knowledge bases related to renal ageing, chronic kidney disease-associated premature ageing, maladaptive repair, renal fibrosis, diabetic kidney disease, tubular epithelial injury, SASP, uremic toxicity, transplantation-related injury, and senescence-targeted interventions. Recent hotspots centered on diabetic kidney disease, acute kidney injury, kidney fibrosis, tubular epithelial cells, DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammaging, immunosenescence, extracellular vesicles, and senolytic therapy. CONCLUSION: Research on cellular senescence-related kidney diseases has shifted from descriptive studies of renal ageing and chronic kidney disease complications toward disease-specific, cell-type-specific, and translational investigations. Future studies should integrate single-cell and spatial multi-omics, establish reliable renal senescence biomarkers, and develop safer kidney-targeted senotherapeutic strategies.

title: Chondrocyte Senescence in Osteoarthritis: Potential Targets and Pharmacological Interventions.
authors: Dunyong Tan; Jiawei Guo; Tianyu Wang; Siyao Yang; Jianquan Liu; Daping Wang; Wencui Li
abstract: PurposeThis review aims to elucidate the mechanisms underlying chondrocyte senescence in osteoarthritis (OA) from 4 core perspectives: extracellular inflammation, mechanical overload and stress, intracellular metabolic and signaling dysregulation, and genetics-related alterations. It further summarizes emerging therapeutic strategies targeting chondrocyte senescence to address the unmet clinical need for disease-modifying OA interventions.FindingsAccumulating evidence indicates that chondrocyte senescence drives OA progression through multiple interconnected mechanisms. These include amplification of inflammation and extracellular matrix degradation via the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), disruption of anabolic-catabolic homeostasis, dysregulation of mechanotransduction pathways under excessive mechanical load, and reshaping of intracellular metabolism and redox balance. Additional contributing mechanisms involve epigenetic dysregulation, non-coding RNA-mediated gene modulation, and impaired autophagy. Therapeutic approaches under preclinical or clinical investigation encompass senolytic and senomorphic agents, chondroprotective biological materials, genetic or RNA-based interventions, as well as strategies targeting SASP modulation and extracellular microenvironment repair.ConclusionsChondrocyte senescence serves as a central convergent mechanism in OA pathogenesis and a promising target for disease-modifying therapies. Advances in mechanistic understanding and senescence-targeted interventions offer new avenues for translational innovation, though critical challenges related to specificity, safety, and long-term efficacy require further resolution.

title: Inflammaging and Cellular Senescence in Postmenopausal Depression: Linking Estrogen Deficiency, Immune Dysregulation, and Brain Aging.
journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology
authors: Lan Zhang; Yao Yao; Xiaoyu Cai
abstract: Postmenopausal depression is clinically heterogeneous and cannot be explained by estrogen deficiency alone. We propose a conceptual, testable neuroimmune-aging model in which endocrine decline may interact with inflammaging, cellular senescence, and brain vulnerability in a subset of women. The evidentiary base is uneven: direct studies of senescence in well-phenotyped postmenopausal depression are lacking; clinical endocrine data come mainly from perimenopausal depression; molecular-senescence findings come from late-life depression or general major depressive disorder; and most cellular and brain mechanisms are supported by aging or preclinical models. Reduced estrogen signaling may weaken immune homeostasis, whereas peripheral cytokines or senescence-associated secretory phenotype factors could influence vascular and neural interfaces, glia, neurotransmitter metabolism, stress signaling, mitochondrial function, and neuroplasticity. These pathways are candidate mediators, not established causal mechanisms. Clinically established care remains diagnosis-based antidepressant treatment, evidence-based management of vasomotor and sleep symptoms, and individualized menopausal hormone therapy for appropriate candidates. Anti-inflammatory, microbiome-based, and senescence-targeted strategies remain investigational; no senolytic or senomorphic is approved for depression or menopause-related mood symptoms. Prospective studies integrating menopausal staging, prespecified confounders, senescence biomarkers, neuroimaging, and mood outcomes are needed to test this model.

title: Identification of cepharanthine as a novel senolytic that selectively eliminates senescent cells by regulating cell survival signaling pathways.
journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology
authors: Yipu Fan; Haokaifeng Wu; Jingke Xie; Jing Wen; Yihan Zhang; Chuang Li; Zhenhua Wang; Luqing Wang; Xiaodong Shu; Chenleng Cai; Jing Liu; Duanqing Pei; Huanxing Su; Dajiang Qin
abstract: BACKGROUND: Senolytics are small-molecule drugs that selectively induce apoptosis in senescent cells, thereby reducing the chronic inflammation and tissue damage caused by the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) and delaying aging, improving organ function and extending healthspan. Existing senolytics, however, often suffer from low bioavailability and off-target toxicity, so potent and safer senolytics are urgently needed. PURPOSE: To screen for novel senolytic compounds and validate the ability of cepharanthine (CEP) to eliminate senescent cells, improve organ function and extend lifespan. STUDY DESIGN: Preclinical study combining in vitro phenotypic screening and mechanistic assays with in vivo validation in zebrafish, C. elegans, naturally aged mice and a Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) mouse model. METHODS: Senolytic efficacy was assessed by a senescent cell-based phenotypic screen, IC₅₀ determination, inhibitor-based rescue assays and multiple senescence models. RNA-seq and pathway enrichment identified the key PI3K/AKT and PERK-ATF4-CHOP pathways, verified by Western blot, qRT-PCR, immunofluorescence and mitochondrial assays. In vivo efficacy was evaluated by senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining, HE staining, immunofluorescence, ELISA, biochemical assays and survival analysis. RESULTS: CEP selectively eliminates senescent cells by cooperatively and in parallel regulating the PI3K/AKT and PERK-ATF4-CHOP pathways, differentially inducing PUMA/NOXA and triggering mitochondrial intrinsic apoptosis. In zebrafish, C. elegans, naturally aged mice and HGPS mice, CEP clears senescent cells, reduces SASP levels, improves organ function and prolongs lifespan. CONCLUSION: CEP is a novel natural senolytic that induces mitochondrial intrinsic apoptosis via parallel, non-redundant regulation of the PI3K/AKT and PERK-ATF4-CHOP pathways, showing good potential for clinical translation.

title: Fisetin attenuates endothelial cells senescence and atherosclerosis via FTO-mediated m6A demethylation of JPX.
authors: Peibing Ge; Jiajia Wu; Yang Zeng; Zequn Zhang; Mengjie Liu; Hailang Liu; Jin Geng
abstract: Endothelial cells (ECs) senescence is a key driver of vascular dysfunction and atherogenesis, underscoring the clinical importance of identifying novel therapeutic agents capable of delaying this process. Fisetin, a natural occurring flavonoid, has shown promising anti-aging potential. Using multiple senescence biomarker assays, the present study revealed that JPX (just proximal to the X-inactive specific transcript), a chromatin-associated regulatory RNA, engages in cooperative interaction with STING-activated p65/BRD4 to promote EC senescence. Mechanistically, m6A modification stabilizes JPX, enabling its interaction with p65 and BRD4 to activate a transcriptional program that drives ECs senescence. Importantly, fisetin promotes FTO-mediated m6A demethylation of JPX, thereby suppressing ECs senescence. In vivo, fisetin treatment significantly extended the lifespan of aged mice and attenuated endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerotic progression. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that fisetin alleviates vascular aging and atherosclerosis through an m6A-dependent mechanism, highlighting its therapeutic potential for age-related cardiovascular diseases.

title: A genome-wide senescence synthetic lethality screen identifies PARP16 as a senolytic target.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
authors: Shohini Ghosh-Choudhary; Jie Liu; Delphine Beaulieu; Ricardo Pineda; Haoxiang Yang; Shria Moturi; Mads B Larsen; Irene Alfaras; Mehdi Pirooznia; Shihui Liu; Jonathan K Alder; Yuan Liu; Bill B Chen; Melanie Königshoff; Toren Finkel
abstract: Accumulation of senescent cells is increasingly viewed as a significant contributor to aging and age-related diseases. To date, the elimination of senescent cells through small molecule senolytic agents has largely relied on a limited number of repurposed agents, often leveraged from previous oncological applications. Here, we describe a CRISPR-based, genome-wide, synthetic lethal screen for senescent cells. From this screen, we identify a number of genes whose deletion appears to be well tolerated in normal proliferating cells, but whose deletion is lethal in the context of senescence. We further characterize one promising candidate gene encoding the ER-resident protein PARP16. Knockdown of PARP16 does not affect the viability of mouse or human cells but results in the death of a wide range of senescent cells. Furthermore, two distinct small molecule PARP16 inhibitors have little effect of normal cell growth but result in the selective death of senescent cells in culture and in freshly isolated human donor lung tissue explants. Together, these results demonstrate a rational strategy to identify novel senolytic therapies that could have potential applications for a wide range of age-related conditions.

title: DNA barcoding and cellular senescence in atherosclerosis: Vascular smooth muscle cell lineage tracing and potential for future Senotherapeutics.
authors: Amitabh C Pandey; Eli Tsakiris
abstract: Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and substantial risk persists even with optimal preventive therapy. Cellular senescence is a state of growth arrest accompanied by a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) and has emerged as a candidate driver of vascular disease states. Recently, vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) have moved from passive bystanders in vascular diseases, including atherosclerosis, to pivotal cells integral to many facets of plaque biology. Within the lesion microenvironment, VSMCs undergo phenotypic switching and de-differentiation into macrophage-like, osteogenic, fibromyocyte, and senescent states, frequently extinguishing canonical lineage markers. However, defining the independent contribution of senescent VSMCs is complicated by two converging problems: the absence of a universal, specific senescence marker, and the loss of identity that accompanies VSMC trans-differentiation. We argue that DNA barcoding, a high-resolution, marker-independent lineage-tracing strategy matured in hematology and oncology, can address both obstacles. Building on the established foundation of multicolor reporters, we contrast static high-diversity libraries with evolving CRISPR-Cas9 recorders and human-translatable retrospective approaches, emphasizing that barcoding reports clonal lineage and must be paired with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics to position the senescent state on a reconstructed clonal tree. We further appraise emerging senotherapeutics, whose inconsistent and occasionally harmful in vivo results reflect a failure to identify the target cell rather than a failure of pharmacology. This distinction argues for lineage-restricted targeting. Integrating clonal barcoding, spatial multi-omics, and senescence atlases may help resolve the role of VSMC senescence in atherogenesis and enable cell-state-specific therapy.

title: Cellular Senescence as a Multiorgan Driver of Diabetes-Associated Cardiovascular and Kidney Disease.
authors: Hongyu Zhang; Jing Feng; Dong Zhu; Jingwei Feng; Jiajun Zhi; Yiwen Deng; Haiyue Jiang
abstract: Cellular senescence may contribute to persistent cardiovascular and kidney dysfunction in diabetes, but its effects depend on cell identity, tissue compartment and disease stage. This targeted narrative review integrates mechanistic, preclinical and early human evidence into a proposed multiorgan framework. Experimental studies support functional effects of senescent beta-cell, adipose, vascular and tubular populations, while predominantly post-mitotic cardiomyocytes and mature podocytes exhibit senescence-like states. Local paracrine mechanisms, including tubular-to-fibroblast signalling, are better established than source-specific transmission between distant organs. Adipose-derived extracellular vesicles provide an experimental adipose-to-heart example in diabetic mice, whereas the broader contributions of circulating SASP factors, metabolites and immune-cell trafficking remain incompletely resolved. We therefore present the diabetes-heart-kidney senescence loop as a conceptual interpretation of the available evidence, rather than a validated causal network. Senolytic and senomorphic interventions improve selected phenotypes in preclinical models. Major unresolved questions concern the pathogenic cell populations in patients, the direction and specificity of interorgan signalling, and the timing and safety of intervention. Clinical translation requires cell-resolved biomarkers and evidence that senescence-directed treatment adds functional benefit to established cardiometabolic care while preserving beneficial repair and immune functions.

title: Targeting microglial senescence in brain ageing and Alzheimer's disease: Mechanistic evidence and the therapeutic potential of natural products.
authors: Shashi Alok
abstract: Microglial senescence is a candidate contributor to brain ageing and Alzheimer's disease, but its identification and therapeutic tractability remain contested. Activation, lysosomal expansion, lipid accumulation and dystrophic morphology do not independently establish senescence. This review critically examines how uncertainty in state identification affects mechanistic interpretation and natural-product evaluation. Genetic perturbation, human induced pluripotent stem cell models and pharmacological studies connect mitochondrial proteotoxic stress, impaired autophagy, DNA damage and sustained inflammatory signalling with senescence-associated microglial phenotypes. Disease-associated and senescence-associated microglial populations are not interchangeable. Delphinidin, andrographolide, resveratrol, honokiol, rosmarinic acid and cycloastragenol reduce senescence-associated readouts in selected experimental systems. Current evidence mainly supports prevention or phenotype modulation; selective microglial senolysis, durable reversal and senescence-dependent cognitive rescue remain unestablished. Functional assessment requires substrate specificity: impaired harmful-substrate disposal can coexist with excessive synaptic engulfment. Translation requires achievable unbound brain exposure, treatment after phenotype establishment and models relevant to human ageing. Circulating inflammatory-marker changes alone cannot demonstrate drug action within microglia or modification of their senescence-associated state. Small, uncontrolled senolytic trials support the feasibility of treatment administration and preliminary pharmacological assessment, but do not establish cognitive efficacy or selective action on senescent microglia. Progress depends on convergent state identification, delayed intervention, lineage-resolved causal experiments and exposure-matched pharmacology. Natural products remain useful mechanistic probes and potential therapeutic leads whose value should be judged by restoration of protective microglial functions and neural outcomes, rather than marker suppression alone.

title: Senolytic drug reduces cancer resistance to PD-L1 blockade.
authors: Nourridine Siewe; Avner Friedman
abstract: Resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), including anti-PD-L1 therapies, remains a major challenge in cancer treatment, with many patients relapsing despite initial responses. Here, we develop a mathematical model to investigate a mechanism of anti-PD-L1 resistance driven by age-associated senescence of CD8+ T cells, in which senescent T cells (Ts) secrete VEGF, thereby promoting tumor growth through enhanced vascular support. To counteract this effect, we incorporate the senolytic drug navitoclax (ABT-263), which selectively eliminates senescent T cells, and evaluate the efficacy of combined senolytic-anti-PD-L1 therapy in extending tumor remission. Model predictions are validated against independent murine data involving navitoclax and anti-PD-L1 treatment. The model is used to study different strategies of combining the senolytic drug with anti-PD-L1, in order to maximize the remission time of the combined treatment. The optimal starting time of the treatment with the senolytic drug depends on the senescent-to-functional T cells ratio, Ts/T. The paper identifies immune senescence as an important determinant of response to cancer immunotherapy.

title: The senescent tumor microenvironment: Roles in glioblastoma progression.
journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Reviews on cancer
authors: Yurui Zhang; Yitong Li; Yudi Wang; Yucui Dong
abstract: In adults, glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common malignant primary tumor of the brain and other central nervous system sites and is linked to older age and generally poor outcomes. Chronological aging and cellular senescence are distinct processes, but both can reshape the GBM tumor microenvironment (TME). Following radiotherapy or chemotherapy, both malignant and non-malignant cells may enter a senescence-associated state. When these cells persist, their senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) may reshape the extracellular matrix (ECM), maintain inflammation, and support residual tumor-cell survival, stem-like plasticity, and treatment resistance. Age-associated or senescence-associated changes also occur in immune and stromal compartments, although bona fide cellular senescence has not been established uniformly across T cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and fibroblast-associated populations. This review focuses on how cellular senescence, particularly therapy-induced senescence, reshapes the GBM microenvironment through SASP signaling and how these effects intersect with age-associated remodeling of tumor, stromal, extracellular-matrix, and immune compartments. We also discuss senescence-inducing therapies, senolytic and SASP-directed strategies, and the major challenges to their clinical translation. Current evidence supports biomarker-guided targeting of defined post-treatment SASP pathways and temporally controlled senolytic intervention as promising translational directions, while blood-brain barrier penetration, senescence heterogeneity, and off-target effects in normal neural tissue remain major challenges.

title: Phenolic Phytonutrients and Brain Mitochondrial Function in Aging: From Flavonoids to Phenolic Monoterpenoids.
authors: Khadidja Kessas; Touria Hadj Slimane; Nouria Hallal; Zhor Chouari; Imen Ghzaeil; Amira Zarrouk; Omar Kharoubi
abstract: Brain mitochondrial dysfunction is a core, early feature of ageing, driven by bioenergetic decline, cardiolipin peroxidation, membrane phospholipid remodelling and chronic neuroinflammation. Several dietary phenolics have been linked to components of this cycle in preclinical models, yet their mechanistic relationships are rarely examined together. This critical review covers six compounds spanning three chemical families: the flavonoids quercetin and rutin, the phenolic acids gallic and caffeic acids, and the phenolic monoterpenoids thymol and carvacrol. Evidence is organised around four mechanistic axes (mitochondrial bioenergetics, Nrf2-mediated redox signalling, mitochondrial dynamics/mitophagy/biogenesis, and intrinsic apoptotic signalling), comparing all six directly rather than as separate monographs. The review also addresses the structural lipid context: cardiolipin, phosphatidylserine and DHA-enriched phospholipid species in age-related neuronal vulnerability. Across all six, Keap1-Nrf2 activation is the most consistently documented mechanism; this finding is specific to these phenolics and should not be generalised to dietary polyphenols as a class. Quercetin has the most developed evidence on the quality-control axis, encompassing PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, fusion/fission dynamics and PGC-1α-driven biogenesis; comparable data for gallic acid, caffeic acid, thymol and carvacrol on these pathways remain sparse. A targeted literature search found no peer-reviewed neuronal confirmation of PGC-1α induction magnitudes reported for thymol and carvacrol, flagged here as a research priority. For quercetin, bioavailability constraints are the primary translational barrier; for the remaining five, the mechanistic profile requires further development. Clinical evidence is limited to early-phase senolytic trials for quercetin and a single dietary-dose randomised controlled trial showing a reaction-time benefit.

title: Immunosenescence in Metabolic Disorders: From Cellular Mechanisms to Therapeutic Strategies.
authors: Dong Guo; Qingqing Chen; Hong Cai; Yiyu Lu
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This review comprehensively examines the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the crosstalk between metabolic disorders and immunosenescence and elucidates the fundamental roles of clonal hematopoiesis (CH) and immune surveillance while critically evaluating both classical and emerging therapeutic strategies that target these pathways. RECENT FINDINGS: Recent evidence indicates that immune cells displaying senescence-associated phenotypes accumulate in adipose tissue, liver, and vasculature, where they exhibit mitochondrial dysfunction, epigenetic remodeling, and a maladaptive senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) driven by NF-κB and C/EBPβ. Key SASP components, including interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and CCL2, together with p53/p21- and p16/RB-mediated cell-cycle arrest and cGAS-STING pathway activation, contribute to adipocyte hypertrophy, insulin resistance, hepatic steatosis, and dyslipidemia. These changes are associated with the accelerated progression of obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), and atherosclerosis. Additionally, CH and impaired immune surveillance exacerbate chronic metabolic inflammation. This review discusses classical interventions, including metabolic modulators, senolytics, and senomorphics, alongside emerging strategies such as Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTAC)-based senolytics, CH-targeted approaches, and mitochondrial-targeted therapies, emphasizing mechanistic differences and supporting clinical evidence. Nevertheless, challenges related to achieving tissue-specific delivery while minimizing systemic toxicity remain unresolved. Immunosenescence plays a dual role; transient and context-dependent SASP signaling can contribute to tissue repair, whereas persistent or dysregulated SASP activity can promote pathology. Currently, validated clinical tools for assessing immune-driven metabolic dysfunction are lacking. This absence of standardized evaluation frameworks hinders the translation of these therapies into clinical practice, highlighting the necessity for a theoretical foundation to guide precision treatment of obesity-related metabolic diseases and to promote healthy aging.

title: Pharmacological targeting of ageing hallmarks: molecular mechanism and clinical translation.
authors: Lin Su; Hongyao Li; Xiuying Yan
abstract: Background: Ageing is a gradual biological process characterized by progressive physiological decline and increased susceptibility to age-related diseases. The hallmarks of ageing provide a mechanistic framework for understanding these changes and identifying potential therapeutic targets. Objective: This review summarizes the major hallmarks of ageing, their links to age-related diseases, and pharmacological strategies targeting these mechanisms. Methods: We provide a narrative synthesis of current mechanistic and clinical evidence on candidate gerotherapeutics. Results: Pharmacological interventions targeting nutrient sensing, cellular senescence, mitochondrial dysfunction, and other aging-related pathways include metformin, rapamycin, senotherapeutics, and NAD+ precursors. These agents show potential to improve healthspan and reduce disease burden, although human evidence remains heterogeneous. Conclusion: Targeting the hallmarks of ageing represents a promising therapeutic strategy, but further well-designed clinical studies are needed to establish efficacy, safety, and clinically meaningful benefits.

title: Fisetin attenuates TBHP-induced senescence-associated phenotypes in human gingival fibroblasts and is associated with reduced p53/p21 expression.
authors: Minshan Chen; Jianbo Sun; Kaiyin Chen
abstract: Fisetin has potential anti-ageing activity, but its effects on human gingival fibroblast (HGF) senescence remain unclear. This study investigated fisetin using network pharmacology, molecular docking, and in vitro assays. Network analysis predicted fisetin-related targets enriched in cellular senescence, PI3K-Akt signalling, extracellular matrix remodelling, and inflammation pathways, with TP53, AKT1, and matrix metalloproteinases as potential key nodes. Docking suggested favourable binding of fisetin to core targets, particularly TP53. In tert-butyl hydroperoxide-induced HGFs, fisetin improved migration, reduced senescence-associated beta-galactosidase positivity, and decreased p53 and p21 protein expression. Fisetin also reduced MMP1 and MMP9 mRNA levels while restoring COL1A1 and COL3A1 mRNA expression. In a separate lipopolysaccharide-stimulated inflammation model, fisetin reduced interleukin-6 secretion. These findings suggest that fisetin attenuates selected senescence-associated phenotypes in HGFs, accompanied by reduced p53/p21 expression and improved extracellular matrix-related marker profiles, warranting further validation in tissue-level, animal, and clinical studies in future work, although causal mediation was not established.

title: Retraction notice to "Fisetin as a caloric restriction mimetic protects rat brain against aging induced oxidative stress, apoptosis and neurodegeneration" [Life Sci. 193 (2018) 171-179].
authors: Sandeep Singh; Abhishek Kumar Singh; Geetika Garg; Syed Ibrahim Rizvi

title: Radiation-induced atrial fibrillation is driven by cellular senescence via the GATA4 - NF-κB pathway and rescued by D/Q senolytic therapy.
authors: Chao Zhang; Huai Lan; Liming Yu; Jikai Zhao; Tao Huang; Boxuan Sun; Shan Meng; Jinfeng Duan; Jing Liu; Zijun Zhou; Zhishang Wang; Jiahui Li; Xinyi Huang; Huishan Wang
abstract: Radiation-induced heart disease is a well-recognized complication of thoracic radiotherapy, with atrial fibrillation (AF) being a particularly notable sequela. The mechanisms by which ionizing radiation (IR) heightens susceptibility to AF remain inadequately understood. This study seeks to elucidate the role of cellular senescence and the GATA4-NF-κB signaling pathway in radiation-induced atrial remodeling and the pathogenesis of AF. An in vivo mouse model was developed through localized cardiac irradiation using 20 Gy X-rays. The irradiated mice demonstrated dose-dependent atrial structural and electrophysiological remodeling. Transcriptomic analysis revealed significant enrichment in DNA damage response (DDR), NF-κB signaling, and aging-related pathways. IR exposure induced substantial DNA damage, activated ATM/ATR pathways, and enhanced autophagic flux. These responses culminated in the accumulation of GATA4 and phosphorylation of NF-κB, which drove the expression of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), coinciding with increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity. In vitro, these crucial findings were recapitulated using irradiated HL-1 atrial cardiomyocytes, whereas the knockdown of GATA4 effectively suppressed both cellular senescence and SASP expression. Notably, treatment with the senolytic combination of dasatinib and quercetin (D/Q) alleviated DNA damage, inhibited excessive autophagy, and suppressed the GATA4-NF-κB pathway in irradiated mice, thereby reducing SASP levels. These improvements resulted in the reversal of atrial structural and electrophysiological remodeling and a marked reduced susceptibility to AF. Overall, our findings demonstrate that IR promotes atrial remodeling by inducing DNA damage-mediated cellular senescence via the GATA4-NF-κB-SASP axis. Targeting this pathway with senolytics such as D/Q thus identifies a promising therapeutic strategy for preventing radiation-induced atrial fibrillation.

title: Discovery of a quinoline-based senomorphic agent for the treatment of chronic kidney disease.
authors: Youyou Chen; Sicong Qiao; Xin Chen; Linfen Li; Jiale Wu; Centao Shi; Jian Li; Yuan Guo; Yunyuan Huang; Wenwen Liu
abstract: Senescence is a risk factor for chronic diseases, making anti-aging interventions a promising strategy for geriatric conditions. While a non-antibacterial derivative C1 of enrofloxacin has been proposed to extend lifespan in Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans), its unresolved cytotoxicity in healthy mammalian cells limits its combinatory potential and safety as an anti-aging agent. With the aim of preserving anti-aging activity while enhancing safety, we here performed structural optimization of C1 and created 37 derivatives. Among them, C36, which derived from introducing an isopropoxy group at the R7 position, exhibited the most potent lifespan extending effect (11.49%) in C. elegans with low cytotoxicity (IC50 > 100 μM) in two commonly used aging relevant mammalian cell lines. In a mouse model with doxorubicin induced senescence, C36 treatment attenuated the senescence associated secretory phenotype (SASP), mitigated cell cycle arrest, and significantly lowered aging markers in kidney tissue. Given the central role of cellular senescence and SASP in the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD), we evaluated C36 in mice with kidney failure. The results showed that C36 effectively reduced the level of SASP and thus alleviated senescence of the diseased kidney through a senomorphic approach. In comparison to the model group, C36 significantly improved renal function, reduced renal fibrosis by approximately 50%, and decreased the renal expression of the senescence-associated markers p21, p16, and p53. These findings imply that C36 could have a role in modulating organismal senescence with potential implications for CKD, and offer a perspective on drug repurposing and secondary development for age-related diseases.

title: Nanotherapeutic Strategies Targeting Senescent Microenvironment for Aging-Related Chronic Diseases.
authors: Jing Ma; Xueying Li; Zhijing He; Xue Sun; Guangyao Lv
abstract: DCellular senescence is a central driver of age-related chronic diseases, including neurodegeneration, atherosclerosis, metabolic disorders, and fibrosis. The persistent accumulation of senescent cells and their associated secretory phenotype (SASP) creates a shared microenvironmental basis for disease progression across multiple organ systems. Senolytic and senomorphic strategies targeting senescent cells have shown therapeutic promise, yet their clinical translation remains constrained by insufficient targeting specificity, off-target toxicity, and poor tissue penetration. Nanotechnology-enabled delivery systems offer a programmable approach to overcome these barriers through rationally designed carriers that enable selective recognition of senescent cells, microenvironment-responsive drug release, and enhanced tissue accessibility. This review develops an integrated framework that links nanoplatform design principles to mechanistic intervention categories and disease-specific evidence. We first outline the molecular basis of cellular senescence and its pathological roles in age-related diseases. We then systematically examine four mechanistic dimensions of nanotherapeutic intervention in the senescent microenvironment: redox homeostasis modulation, inflammatory reprogramming, senescent cell clearance, and immune surveillance reactivation. These dimensions target reactive oxygen species, pro-inflammatory cytokines, senescent cells, and immune effector cells, respectively. Representative nanoplatforms applied to neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, metabolic, musculoskeletal, and fibrotic diseases are discussed. We further analyze key translational challenges, including senescent cell heterogeneity, impaired drug delivery in aged tissues, and regulatory uncertainty. Finally, we discuss emerging directions in precision rejuvenation, offering a conceptual framework for the next generation of senescence-targeted nanotherapies.

title: Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (SASP) and Atherosclerotic Plaque Inflammation: Natural Product-Based Interventions and Implications for Personalized Therapy.
authors: Dekun Liu; Napamanee Kornthong; Shuguang Yu; Jakkree Tangthianchaichana; Prasert Sobhon; Sha Yang
abstract: Atherosclerosis underlies most ischemic cardiovascular events, and its prevalence rises with population aging. Cellular senescence is increasingly implicated as a driver of plaque progression, although the causal evidence is largely preclinical. Senescent endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and macrophages acquire a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), releasing cytokines, chemokines, proteases, and procoagulant factors. These factors sustain plaque inflammation, weaken the fibrous cap, and increase rupture risk. In this narrative review, we link SASP signaling to plaque instability through NF-κB, p38 MAPK, mTOR, NLRP3, and cGAS-STING signaling. We then evaluate tetramethylpyrazine (ligustrazine), quercetin, fisetin, resveratrol, and curcumin against an operational definition reserving senolytic and senomorphic for effects shown in confirmed senescent cells. On that standard, only quercetin and fisetin qualify; for the other three, the vascular evidence is anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, or senescence-preventive rather than directed at established senescent cells. Tetramethylpyrazine protects the endothelial glycocalyx and reduces plaque area in atherosclerotic rabbits. Dasatinib plus quercetin benefits ApoE-/- mice, whereas the only human evidence comes from quercetin monotherapy, which improved endothelium-dependent vasodilation in vessels from symptomatic male, but not female, bypass patients ex vivo. Because senescence burden varies between individuals, we consider how multiomics profiling might stratify patients. The evidence remains mechanistic and hypothesis-generating, with limited human cardiovascular interventional data: Much of it was recorded in cells never shown to be senescent, and no formulation has been shown to reach the human vessel wall. Targeting the SASP therefore requires trial evidence rather than an established basis for precision medicine.

title: Enabling Photoacoustic Imaging and Photothermal Elimination of Senescent Cells via an Activatable Theranostic Probe.
authors: Chong-Hua Zhang; Sha Zeng; Yu-Yan Sun; Luyang Chen; Jiaqi Hao; Hu Zhou; Xianjun Liu
abstract: Excessive accumulation of senescent cells disrupts tissue homeostasis, induces chronic inflammation and tumorigenesis, and ultimately accelerates senescence-associated dysfunction and malignant progression. Developing reliable tools for the detection and elimination of senescent cells is critical for the precise diagnosis and timely intervention of aging-associated diseases. However, existing senolytic theranostic probes suffer from oxygen-dependent photodynamic therapy (PDT) efficacy and the inherent limitations of fluorescence imaging in penetration depth and spatial resolution. Herein, we report the first theranostic probe RPM-Gal that integrates senescence-associated β-galactosidase-activated photoacoustic imaging and photothermal elimination of senescent cells. RPM-Gal is assembled by tethering a β-D-galactopyranoside moiety to a rhodol-derived polymethine scaffold (RPM-OH) via a self-immolative benzyl spacer. In vitro tests demonstrate that RPM-Gal possesses an excellent photoacoustic response and outstanding photothermal behavior against β-galactosidase. It is found that the overexpressed β-galactosidase in senescent cells can specifically activate the PA signal and the PTT effect of RPM-Gal upon light irradiation. This probe has been further successfully implemented for PA imaging and photothermal elimination of senescent tumor cells in vivo, establishing a targeted avenue for effective senolytic therapy.

title: The neuro-inflammaging triangle: a self-amplifying circuit of protein pathology, senescence-associated secretory phenotype and innate immunity in neurodegenerative disease.
authors: He-Jin Lee; Seung-Jae Lee
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, share common pathological features, including abnormal protein aggregation, chronic neuroinflammation and progressive neuronal loss. Ageing is the strongest risk factor, accompanied by a chronic, mild inflammatory state called 'inflammaging,' partly due to senescent cells producing senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors. Innate immune DNA- and danger-sensing pathways, most notably the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway and NOD-like receptor family, pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasomes, convert cellular injury into chronic neuroinflammation. Here, we propose that protein pathology, SASP, and innate immune activation form a self-amplifying triangular circuit leading to age-related neurodegeneration. We present the cellular and molecular basis of each part and how microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells and neurons contribute. We outline treatment strategies, including senolytics, senomorphics, innate immune pathway inhibitors and metabolic restoration, and identify unresolved questions, including the reversibility of post-mitotic neuronal senescence, the relative contribution of each cell type and the translational challenge of interrupting the cycle. Collectively, the neuro-inflammaging triangle theory shifts focus from individual pathogenic entities to the self-amplifying circuit that sustains them, offering a unified mechanistic model to advance our understanding and treatment of age-related neurodegeneration.

title: Cellular Senescence Phenotypes in Cardiovascular Aging: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential.
authors: Pei Mo; Yunmei Li; Yonghong Chen; Yunyun Liang
abstract: Cardiovascular aging emerges from interactions among cumulative stress, cell type-specific senescence programs, and tissue remodeling. This narrative review uses an evidence-weighted, cell-resolved framework to distinguish marker-based associations from causal perturbation studies and to map therapeutic claims to their stage of development. Literature identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PMC through 15 September 2026 was prioritized for cardiovascular relevance, recent mechanistic insight, human data, and experimental rigor. Across endothelial cells, vascular smooth muscle cells, cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, immune cells, and progenitor populations, senescence is not a uniform state: the markers, secretory programs, and functional consequences vary with cell identity and context. Convergent in vitro and animal evidence supports roles for DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, altered nutrient sensing, impaired proteostasis, and inflammatory signaling, whereas human cardiovascular evidence remains predominantly tissue-based or observational. The senescence-associated secretory phenotype can propagate inflammation, matrix remodeling, and secondary senescence, but its composition and biological effect are time- and context-dependent. Senolytics, senomorphics, metabolic modulators, and immune-based approaches have produced encouraging preclinical findings. Small human studies outside cardiovascular indications establish feasibility rather than cardiovascular efficacy, and no senescence-targeted therapy has yet shown clinical benefit for a cardiovascular indication. Progress therefore depends on multidimensional biomarkers, explicit evidence standards, cell- and stage-specific target selection, and trials with cardiovascular functional endpoints. This synthesis identifies these requirements as the practical bridge between mechanistic plausibility and clinically testable senotherapy.

title: Senescence-targeted engineered CAR-T immunotherapy: advances, challenges and perspectives for engineered senolytic immunotherapy.
authors: Jiayu Liu; Wenxia Shao; Qing Ye
abstract: Cellular senescence acts as a core driver of chronic diseases and tissue degeneration. Conventional small-molecule senolytics face critical limitations including poor target specificity and off-target toxicity when eliminating heterogeneous senescent cell populations. This review systematically discusses senescence-targeted engineered chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T immunotherapy, which achieves targeted clearance of pathological senescent cells by recognising specific surface markers. It summarises target-antigen evaluation frameworks, analyzes aged immunosuppressive microenvironment barriers and corresponding engineering strategies, and outlines composite efficacy assessment systems and tiered biomarker-monitoring workflows. Key translational bottlenecks such as imperfect antigen specificity and immune escape are also addressed. Preclinical studies verify organ function restoration and healthspan extension, while clinical evidence remains limited. Future integration of CAR-T technology with smart nanocarriers, synthetic biology and artificial intelligence will promote its clinical translation for senescence-associated disorders.

title: Premature Senescence and Cardiovascular Disease Following Cancer Treatments: Mitochondria-Mediated Mechanistic Insights.
authors: Sudhir Pandey
abstract: The remarkable enhancement in cancer survival attained over recent decades has shifted attention toward the long-term cardiovascular effects of anticancer therapies. Beyond overt cardiotoxicity, accumulating evidence indicates that many conventional chemotherapeutics, including radiotherapy, targeted agents, and emerging immunotherapies, accelerate biological aging of the cardiovascular system through the induction of premature cellular senescence. Senescent endothelial cells, cardiomyocytes, vascular smooth muscle cells, cardiac fibroblasts, and resident immune cells exhibit persistent growth arrest accompanied by metabolic reprogramming, chronic inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and acquisition of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), collectively contributing to adverse cardiac remodeling, vascular dysfunction, myocardial fibrosis, and accelerated atherosclerosis. Among the interconnected mechanisms driving therapy-induced senescence, mitochondria have emerged as central regulators integrating oxidative stress, DNA damage responses, bioenergetic alterations, impaired mitophagy, mitochondrial dynamics, calcium dysregulation, and innate immune activation. Through the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), chronic inflammatory signaling, the release of mitochondrial DNA, and the activation of inflammasomes, dysfunctional mitochondria actively amplify senescence rather than acting only as organelles that produce energy. This creates self-sustaining feed-forward loops that promote cardiovascular aging long after cancer treatment is completed. This review critically examines the molecular mechanisms linking anticancer therapies to premature cardiovascular senescence with particular emphasis on mitochondria-centered signaling networks. I address therapy-specific mitochondrial alterations induced by HER2-targeted treatments, immune checkpoint inhibitors, ionizing radiation, platinum-based drugs, anthracyclines, and more recent anticancer modalities, emphasizing interconnected pathways despite disparate fundamental mechanisms of action. Emerging biomarkers of mitochondrial dysfunction and senescence, together with therapeutic prospects involving senolytics, senomorphics, mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, metabolic modulators, and interventions reestablishing mitochondrial quality control, are also evaluated. Finally, I identify unresolved questions limiting clinical translation and propose future research directions aimed at preserving cardiovascular health in the rapidly expanding population of cancer survivors.

title: The stroma-vascular compartment: central facilitator of the damage response and repair across organs.
authors: Wesley T Abplanalp; Amparo Acker-Palmer; Sofia-Iris Bibli; Ralf P Brandes; Thomas Braun; Sebastian Cremer; Ivan Dikic; Stefanie Dimmeler; Ingrid Fleming; Jasmin Hefendehl; Jiong Hu; Florian Leuschner; Guillermo Luxán; Christian Münch; Stefan Offermanns; Jochen Pöling; Michael Potente; Flavia Rezende; Katrin Schäfer; Marcel H Schulz; Marta Segarra; Mauro Siragusa; Nina Wettschureck; Ilka Wittig
abstract: Tissue injury initiates a complex, multicellular programme whose outcome i.e. functional repair or irreversible fibrosis, is determined by the coordinated activity of the stroma-vascular compartment (SVC). This network of resident fibroblasts, vascular mural cells, endothelial cells and immune populations acts as a gatekeeper of tissue integrity. Following ischaemia, trauma, or mechanical damage, extracellular danger signals are sensed by pattern-recognition receptors and transduced into cell type-specific metabolic and mechanical responses. An initial inflammatory wave clears cellular debris, after which endothelial sprouting and matrix deposition proceed toward scar maturation; a collagen-rich structure whose geometry ultimately governs future perfusion. Epigenetic reprogramming and metabolic rewiring enforce each of these transitions while simultaneously imprinting a memory that skews subsequent responses in the context of ageing, diabetes, chronic inflammation or clonal haematopoiesis. Targeting the SVC, rather than the parenchyma alone, now underpins therapeutic strategies spanning precision senolytics, engineered stromal cell grafts, and biomechanically instructive scaffolds.

title: Cellular Senescence and White-Matter Injury: A Proposed Glial Cascade in AD and Cerebral SVD.
authors: Ximing Li; Hanying Xu; Ying Zhang; Dongxu Li; Wenchuan Wang; Yang Wu; Qingjie Li; Hongmei Nan
abstract: Cellular senescence is one of the hallmarks of aging and has been implicated in age-related neurological disorders, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) and cerebral small-vessel disease (SVD). AD and SVD frequently coexist and both become more common with age, so an age-dependent mechanism may contribute to both. Although their upstream pathologies differ, both can damage white matter. This review proposes a cascade in which microglial senescence may sustain inflammation in white matter and impair myelin debris clearance. In this environment, oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) may differentiate poorly, limiting remyelination, while senescence-like changes within these cells may compound this deficit. Senescent brain endothelial cells may also damage white matter through blood-brain barrier disruption, microvascular rarefaction, reduced perfusion, and impaired neurovascular coupling. Because barrier leakage activates microglia and poor perfusion may limit metabolic support to the oligodendrocyte lineage, these vascular changes could aggravate glial dysfunction. This review integrates evidence scattered across different models and diseases, examining each link in the proposed cascade in turn. The full sequence has not yet been demonstrated in a single experimental system or in humans. In animal models, eliminating or modulating senescent cells has improved pathology or cognition, and restoring aged OPC function has enhanced remyelination. In people, senolytic trials have assessed safety and drug exposure but have not yet established clinical benefit. White-matter injury may serve as a measurable endpoint shared by AD and SVD, and cellular senescence remains a potential contributor to this injury.

title: Mechanisms and disease implications of inflammaging and potential therapeutic strategies.
authors: Xiaotong Song; Shirui Li; Ziheng Jiang; Anshun Yang; Qianqian Lu; Min Fang
abstract: Inflammaging is a chronic, low-grade inflammatory state associated with aging and age-related diseases. This review examines the mechanisms underlying inflammaging, emphasizing the interplay between oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, DNA damage, cellular senescence, and immune dysregulation. Persistent cellular stress promotes senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), while impaired immune clearance allows senescent cells to accumulate, sustaining a self-amplifying inflammatory cycle. We further discuss the involvement of inflammaging in neurodegenerative, infectious, autoimmune, cardiometabolic, and musculoskeletal diseases. Finally, we summarize current and emerging interventions, including lifestyle modifications, pharmacological approaches, senolytics, senomorphics, and strategies targeting mitochondrial quality control and cellular metabolism. Understanding the interconnected mechanisms and tissue-specific effects of inflammaging may facilitate the development of targeted interventions to mitigate age-related diseases and promote healthy aging.

title: Cellular senescence remodels the neuro-immune-tumour niche in neuroblastoma through SASP and core signalling pathways.
journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Reviews on cancer
authors: Zhihan Zhang; Xiaoling Zhang
abstract: Neuroblastoma (NB), the most common extracranial solid tumour in children, presents a stark clinical dichotomy: stage 4S disease may spontaneously regress, whereas high-risk patients face persistently high relapse and mortality rates despite intensive therapy. This suggests that the tumour microenvironment (TME) critically governs disease trajectory. Cellular senescence, a stress-responsive cell fate, has been increasingly implicated in NB, yet its dual pro- and anti-tumourigenic roles remain unclear. Senescence is not uniform; rather, distinct induction conditions generate divergent senescence-associated secretory phenotypes (SASPs), which exert context-dependent paracrine effects on neural, immune, and tumour cells within the TME. This review examines how senescence-driven SASP may remodel the neuro-immune-tumour microenvironment. We outline the triggers and cellular origins of senescence, characterize SASP composition and transcriptional control, and describe its potential multifaceted effects on immune reprogramming, neuroinflammation, and tumour progression. Integrating PI3K/Akt/mTOR and autophagy-apoptosis signalling, along with adjacent neurogenic signals such as SP/NK-1R, we hypothesize that the contrasting outcomes of 4S versus high-risk disease reflect alternative fate switches among senescence, autophagy, and apoptosis. We also summarize emerging senolytic, senomorphic, and neuroimmune-targeted strategies, along with their clinical prospects. A deeper understanding of senescence heterogeneity in neuroblastoma may offer both biological insights and new therapeutic avenues.

title: Therapy-induced tumour senescence drives oxaliplatin resistance via ADORA1-dependent palmitic acid metabolic reprogramming in colorectal cancer.
authors: Yuqin Long; Xue Li; Yunxi Zhu; Yang Shen; Xiaotian Zhou; Ziqin Wei; Yin Yue; Jie Zhang; Changhong Miao
abstract: Oxaliplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) is increasingly used in locally advanced colorectal cancer (CRC); however, early acquired resistance substantially limits its efficacy. We revealed an enrichment of therapy-induced senescence (TIS)-like phenotypes in short-term oxaliplatin-exposed CRC. Consistently, a similar upregulation of senescence markers was observed in oxaliplatin-resistant CRC cells. Senolytic treatment attenuated senescence features and restored oxaliplatin sensitivity in vitro and in vivo. Integrative analysis of RNA-sequencing data from resistant tumours and ABT263-treated resistant tumours identified adenosine A1 receptor (ADORA1) as a key mediator of senescence and oxaliplatin resistance. ADORA1 is highly expressed in CRC tumours and is further induced by oxaliplatin, with elevated ADORA1 levels enriched in chemoresistant patients and associated with poor outcomes following chemotherapy. Mechanistically, ADORA1 directly interacts with and stabilises fatty acid synthase (FASN) by suppressing its ubiquitin-mediated degradation, thereby promoting palmitic acid (PA) synthesis, lipid droplet accumulation and p53/p21-driven senescence. Conversely, ADORA1 knockdown attenuates these phenotypes and restores oxaliplatin sensitivity. Together, these findings identify the ADORA1-FASN-PA metabolic reprogramming as a central mechanistic link between TIS and oxaliplatin resistance in CRC, highlighting this pathway as a promising therapeutic target for overcoming early acquired resistance.

title: Senescent cells in cancer immunity: mechanisms of immune remodeling and opportunities for traditional Chinese medicine-derived senotherapeutics.
authors: Qiuhua Zhang; Huimin Jin; Lingyong Cao; Fangfang Tao
abstract: Cellular senescence has context-dependent effects in cancer. Although transient senescence can suppress malignant proliferation, persistent senescent cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME) may promote tumor progression, immune escape and treatment resistance. How these cells reshape antitumor immunity, and whether traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)-derived interventions can target them, has not been integrated within a translational framework. This Review synthesizes the immune-regulatory activities of pre-existing senescent cells in the TME through three interconnected mechanisms: cell-autonomous immune evasion caused by altered activating and inhibitory surface signals; senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)-driven recruitment and reprogramming of immunosuppressive myeloid and lymphoid populations; and immunosenescence-associated failure of senescent-cell surveillance. We then evaluate TCM-derived natural products and formulas according to their predominant effects on established senescent cells: senomorphic suppression of harmful SASP programs, senolytic elimination of senescent cells, and emerging immune-oriented strategies designed to restore the recognition and clearance of senescent cells. Reductions in SASP-associated inflammation and paracrine tumor support are the most consistently supported endpoints across compounds and experimental models. Evidence linking senolysis to immune remodeling remains limited, whereas immune-mediated clearance has been explored only in preliminary preclinical studies. Across these categories, heterogeneous senescent cell states, inconsistent biomarkers, limited immune-functional endpoints and insufficient standardization of complex formulas constrain mechanistic interpretation and clinical translation. Persistent senescent cells evade immune clearance through altered surface recognition and SASP-mediated immune remodeling, while immunosenescence further weakens host surveillance. These mechanisms identify restoration of senescence surveillance as a therapeutic opportunity. Future studies should investigate TCM-derived natural products as a source of novel senotherapeutics capable of restoring immune recognition and clearance of pre-existing senescent cells, either alone or alongside senomorphic or senolytic activity. This immune-oriented strategy should be validated using direct measures of immune-cell engagement, senescent cell clearance and antitumor efficacy.

title: Bidirectional cellular senescence crosstalk in MASLD: mechanisms, disease progression, and treatment strategies.
authors: Jinchao Shi; Changpu Zhao; Lei Luo; Haoran Wang; Pu Wei; Xiaojing Wang; Zhiwan Tong; Shunyi Zhu; Qing Zhao; Runyu Li; Jia Yan
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is not simply a disorder of hepatocyte lipid storage. As metabolic stress persists, damaged hepatocytes and non-parenchymal cells can enter senescent or senescence-like states that reshape the hepatic microenvironment.
