This review discusses how senescent hepatocytes, hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs), and immune cells interact during progression from MASLD to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Lipotoxicity, oxidative stress and organelle stress, impaired autophagy, and DNA damage promote hepatocyte senescence and senescence-associated hepatocyte-specific gene signatures (SHGS)-defined phenotypes. Senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors, damage-associated molecular patterns, extracellular vesicles (EVs), and matrix-derived signals then sustain reciprocal loops with macrophages and HSCs while also shaping LSEC-centered vascular and immune crosstalk, amplifying inflammation, fibrosis, sinusoidal dysfunction, and failure of immune clearance. Importantly, HSC senescence is context-dependent. Transient arrest may inhibit matrix production, whereas persistent senescent HSCs can promote inflammation and immune escape. We also consider senolytics, senomorphics, restoration of immune surveillance, metabolic and organelle repair, and cell-specific delivery. Because senescence varies across cell types and disease stages, clinical translation will require the identification of relevant cell states using multiple markers and spatial analysis, as well as biomarkers and trial endpoints that distinguish general metabolic improvement from direct disruption of senescence networks.

title: Validation of senescence as a therapeutic target in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) through navitoclax delivery.
journal: Journal of controlled release : official journal of the Controlled Release Society
authors: Yidi Jiang; Shuangmei Li; Elisa A Liehn; Chee Seng Chan; Ji Xin Tan; Tian Xin Phua; Shing Leng Chan; Choon Keong Lee; Xiangliang Lin; Natalie Jun Hui Soh; Gabriele Grassi; Jiong-Wei Wang; Tong Wang; Brijesh Kumar Singh; Madhulika Tripathi; Wei Seong Toh; Victor C Yu; Giorgia Pastorin
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a chronic liver disease characterized by steatosis, inflammation, and progressive fibrosis. Increasing evidence suggests that cellular senescence contributes to MASH progression by promoting lipid accumulation, inflammatory signaling, and fibrogenic responses, highlighting hepatic senescent cells as a potential therapeutic target. Senolytics selectively eliminate senescent cells, but their application in MASH remains insufficiently explored. In this study, we developed in vitro models integrating hepatic lipid accumulation and hepatocyte-macrophage inflammatory crosstalk to facilitate investigation of the contribution of cellular senescence to MASH pathology and to evaluate senescence-targeted interventions. Senescent hepatic cells showed enhanced lipid accumulation and amplified inflammatory signaling with macrophages. Natural Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) derived from adipocytes reduced senescence-associated phenotypes but exhibited context-dependent biological effects, highlighting the limited control over their intrinsic bioactivity. Navitoclax, a senolytic targeting anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins, reduced senescence-associated phenotypes, but its clinical use is limited by its dose-dependent toxicity. Hence, we conceived nano-Cell Vesicle Technology Systems (nCVTs), a biohybrid-based platform combining cell-derived membranes with synthetic lipids for controlled delivery of navitoclax. Navitoclax-loaded nCVTs retained senolytic activity and reduced inflammatory signaling and fibrotic activation in vitro. Importantly, in a Western diet- and fructose-induced (WDF) MASH mouse model, navitoclax-loaded AML-12-derived nCVTs alleviated hepatic lipid accumulation while reducing histopathological activity score and fibrotic profiles. Neither navitoclax formulation reduced platelet counts or hemoglobin concentrations at the tested dose. Collectively, these findings support cellular senescence as a therapeutically relevant target for MASH and identify nCVTs as a promising engineered platform for controlled senolytic delivery.

title: The thioredoxin system in cellular senescence and ageing: From redox homeostasis to therapeutic targeting.
authors: Yang Yu; Yuying Bai; Taihu Wan; Xinglin Tang
abstract: The major characteristics of cellular senescence are stable cell-cycle arrest, accumulation of DNA damage responses, mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic remodeling, and the release of pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors. Redox imbalance plays a significant role in the initiation and maintenance of senescence, and the mammalian thioredoxin system-comprising cytosolic Trx-1, mitochondrial Trx-2, thioredoxin reductases (TrxR1, TrxR2), and the inhibitor TXNIP-is at a key juncture between oxidative stress, cellular ageing, and age-related diseases. Evidence was identified through a structured literature search of PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus from inception to July 2026 using predefined search terms and eligibility criteria. Primary experimental studies in mammalian cells, tissues, or animal models that directly measured senescence markers were prioritised. Reviews, non-mammalian studies, and studies reporting only general oxidative-stress endpoints were included only when they provided essential mechanistic context and are clearly labelled as such. This review focuses primarily on mammalian mechanisms linking the thioredoxin system to senescence initiation, senescence maintenance, inflammaging, tissue dysfunction, and translational geroscience. We distinguish isoform-specific and context-dependent effects of Trx-1, Trx-2, TrxR, and TXNIP. We also discuss therapeutic strategies targeting the thioredoxin system, including redox modulation, isoform-selective inhibitors, senomorphic approaches, and disease-specific interventions. Overall, the thioredoxin system is a significant molecular link between redox homeostasis, cellular senescence, ageing biology, and age-related pathology, and a candidate target for future geroscience interventions, although direct evidence in aged mammals remains limited.

title: Fatty acid desaturation controls cellular fate decisions between senescence and ferroptosis.
authors: Chisaka Kuehnemann; Samantha T Jezak; Bronwyn A Mogck; Niharika Kura; Rushmeen Tariq; Yuheng Che; Maija Vaittinen; Ioannis Siokas; Sharvari Deshpande; Carlyn Guthrie; Xuejuan Tan; Eliezer Aimontche; Aleksandra Aljakna Kahn; Peter Reifsnyder; Gung Lee; Amene Majidipur; Andrew H Kung; Qiaoling Wang; Diana Jurk; Tong Zheng; Andrew S Greenberg; Xiang-Dong Wang; Koji Kitazawa; Gregory Dolnikowski; Yong Cheng; Nirupa R Matthan; Arvind Ramanthan; Jennifer Lee; Daniel Roh; Howard H Chen; Jussi Pihlajamaki; Ron Korstanje; Christopher D Wiley
abstract: When subject to damage or stress, cells develop responses in order to maintain tissue homeostasis. Two such responses are ferroptosis and cellular senescence, but how cells decide between these outcomes remains unclear. Here, we show that senescent cells increase import and membrane levels of multiple polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), but a specific intermediate PUFA, dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA, 20:3ω-6), is reduced. Exogenous repletion of DGLA instead results in cell death by ferroptosis. Senescent cells manifest additional features associated with ferroptosis, including labile iron and expression of lipoxygenases as well as low-level membrane peroxidation. Oral DGLA supplementation lowers markers of senescence in aged mice and improves age-related functional outcomes. Finally, obese humans with lowered DGLA desaturation rates have lower markers of adipose tissue senescence. Together, our data implicate shifts in PUFA metabolism as a driver of decisions between senescence and ferroptosis.

title: Cellular senescence in diabetic retinopathy: Molecular mechanisms and therapeutic targeting.
journal: Advances in ophthalmology practice and research
authors: Wenhui Liu; Jingzhao Gao; Xinyi Zhang; Fuhua Yang; Mingfei Jiao; Jin Chang; Lin Su; Xiaorong Li
abstract: BACKGROUND: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the leading cause of vision loss in the working-age population, traditionally attributed to metabolic disorders and microvascular damage induced by chronic hyperglycemia. Emerging evidence indicates that cellular senescence acts as a critical upstream driver of DR, with senescent cells accumulating in the retina and secreting a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors that promote chronic inflammation, pathological angiogenesis, and disruption of the blood-retinal barrier (BRB). MAIN TEXT: This review adopts a neurovascular unit (NVU) perspective to synthesize cell-type-specific senescence phenotypes in the diabetic retina, emphasizing that endothelial cell, pericyte, retinal pigment epithelium, microglial, and retinal ganglion cell senescence constitute an interconnected pathological network rather than isolated events. NVU-wide senescence establishes a self-reinforcing cycle: senescent endothelial and pericyte dysfunction drives vascular instability; retinal pigment epithelial cells senescence compromises the outer BRB; and glial cell and retinal ganglion cell senescence amplifies neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. We dissect key molecular drivers-oxidative DNA damage, epigenetic reprogramming (miRNA/Sirtuins), mitophagy impairment, and SASP-mediated inflammatory feedforward-and critically evaluate emerging senotherapeutics (senolytics, senomorphics, and precision delivery platforms) within an evidence-graded framework. CONCLUSIONS: Cellular senescence establishes a progressive senescence-inflammation vicious cycle in DR, affecting multiple interconnected cell types within the NVU and causing neurovascular dysfunction. Targeting cellular senescence through senescent cell clearance, SASP inhibition, mitochondrial homeostasis regulation, and epigenetic modulation offers promising new therapeutic directions. With the advancement of novel senotherapeutics and precision technologies, personalized early treatment and retinal repair for DR may become achievable in the future.

title: Transcriptomic Characterization of Cellular Senescence in Human Donor Livers Before Transplantation.
authors: Adam M Thorne; Sabrina Stimmeder; Kirill Ustyantsev; Niels Mulder; Laura Niedernhofer; Ton Lisman; Marco Demaria; Eugene Berezikov; Folkert Kuipers; Vincent E de Meijer
abstract: With an aging donor population, ischemic and inflammatory injury during organ procurement and preservation may be associated with senescence-associated programs influencing graft biology. Although donor type-specific injury patterns are known, their role in driving cellular senescence and downstream inflammatory responses remains unclear. We performed smart-3SEQ bulk RNA-sequencing on human liver tissue obtained from donation after brain death (DBD) and donation after circulatory death (DCD) donors. Senescence-associated transcriptional signatures were assessed using the SenMayo gene panel and a liver-specific senescence-associated secretory phenotype panel. Immunohistochemistry assessed p16 and p21 protein expression. Findings were evaluated in NanoString-based transcriptomic data from an external cohort. Sixty-six livers (24 DBD and 42 DCD) were included. One thousand five hundredforty-eight differentially expressed genes separated DBD and DCD grafts. Functional enrichment analysis showed distinct biological programs, with DBD grafts enriched for metabolic pathways, epithelial proliferation, and angiogenesis regulation, whereas DCD grafts showed enrichment of immune activation, chemokine signaling, and injury-associated pathways. Senescence-associated analyzes recapitulated this separation. Immunohistochemistry showed a higher proportion of p16-positive nuclei in high-risk DCD livers compared with DBD livers (p = 0.038), whereas no significant difference was observed for p21 (p = 0.687). However, tile-level analysis showed significantly higher proportions of both p16- and p21-positive nuclei in DCD livers (p < 0.001). External cohort analysis confirmed donor-type separation across available transcripts and senescence-associated gene panels. Donor type reflects distinct transcriptional states in human donor livers, with senescence-associated profiles overlapping with donor type-specific injury responses. Injury-induced senescence-associated signaling may influence graft function and recipient (patho)physiology, positioning it as a promising modifiable senolytic or senomorphic target in liver transplantation.

title: Altered protein cysteine reactivity in senescent cells is a vulnerability for senolysis to ameliorate aging.
authors: Rong Wu; Fan Yang; Jiacheng Li; Tong Wu; Ruitu Lyu; Junhong Xiang; Xue Gao; Rukang Zhang; Hao Fan; Chunzhao Yin; Jiayi Tu; Zhicheng Xie; Chufan Cai; Freya Q Zhang; Kelly Xue; Jeronimo Najarro; Lei Dong; Rui Su; Angelo Y Meliton; Em Lundberg; Jonah K Chen; Janane Rahbani; Nickolai O Dulin; Nicole Arellano; Jun-Wei B Hughes; Shannon E Elf; Yu-Ying He; Bruce M Bissonnette; Robert B Hamanaka; Gökhan M Mutlu; Judith Campisi; Chuan He; Jing Chen
abstract: How diet shapes aging and age-related diseases marked by senescent cell accumulation remains unclear. Here we report vanadyl sulfate (VS), a mineral dietary supplement, as a senolytic agent. Oral VS ameliorates phenotypes of aging and diverse age-related disorders and extends lifespan in male mice. Integrated functional omics analyses show that senescent cells exhibit globally reduced proteome cysteine reactivity but increased expression and apparent cysteine reactivity of proteins essential for endoplasmic reticulum proteostasis. This redox-proteostasis state is linked to glutathione disulfide (GSSG) accumulation and can be recapitulated by GSSG delivery in nonsenescent cells. Mechanistically, VS inactivates reactive cysteines and promotes disulfide bond formation in senescent cells, leading to protein misfolding, aggregation and ultimately cell death. Glutathione reductase downregulation promotes GSSG accumulation, distinguishing senescent from nonsenescent cells and conferring selective susceptibility to VS. Our findings reveal an exploitable redox-proteostasis vulnerability of senescent cells with therapeutic potential to ameliorate aging.

title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction as a Context-Dependent Driver and Amplifier of the SASP: Targeting the mtDNA-cGAS-STING Axis for Next-Generation Senotherapeutics.
journal: Journal of cellular and molecular medicine
authors: Hamza Kamaran Hama; Mohammed Ali Hama; Musa M Zorab; Amirreza Gholami; Ammar Mohammed Al-Farga
abstract: Cellular senescence combines stable cell-cycle arrest with mitochondrial and innate immune remodelling that shapes the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). This narrative review evaluates mitochondrial dysfunction as a context-dependent initiator or amplifier of senescence and examines mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sensing through cGAS-STING as a driver of SASP regulation. We distinguish mitochondrial damage, cytosolic mtDNA exposure, pathway activation, SASP transcription, secretion, paracrine activity and tissue outcomes as separate levels of evidence. The strongest mechanistic studies link BAX/BAK-mediated minority mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization, VDAC1 oligomerization, defective mitophagy or abnormal mtDNA composition to cytosolic mtDNA, cGAS-STING activation and SASP modulation through genetic or pharmacological perturbation. However, pathway architecture varies across cell types, tissues and senescence triggers, and nuclear DNA, micronuclei, retroelements and mitochondrial RNA can activate overlapping inflammatory programmes. Preclinical evidence therefore supports STING inhibition primarily as a senomorphic, anti-inflammatory and tissue-protective strategy rather than a senolytic intervention. Mitophagy enhancement, inhibition of mtDNA release, targeted protein degradation and precision delivery offer complementary approaches, but human efficacy remains unestablished. Clinical translation will require standardized biomarkers, biologically informed patient selection, pharmacodynamic confirmation, tissue-restricted or reversible modulation and prospective assessment of antiviral, antitumour and long-term safety. Overall, the mitochondrial dysfunction-mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis is a mechanistically credible but context-dependent therapeutic framework whose clinical value will depend on validated pathway engagement and appropriately timed clinical intervention.

title: The Vicious Cycle of Sleep Disruption and Inflammaging: Mechanisms, Consequences, and Therapeutic Opportunities.
authors: Fu-Ying Zhao; Jia-Mei Wang; Shi-Yang Lu; Liang Hao; Hai-Yan Zhang; Hua-Qin Wang
abstract: Aging is characterized by two interdependent hallmarks: a chronic low-grade inflammatory state known as inflammaging, and a progressive deterioration of sleep and circadian rhythms. Emerging evidence indicates that these are not merely parallel processes but are mechanistically intertwined in a self-perpetuating cycle. This review synthesizes current knowledge on how age-related sleep and circadian disturbances exacerbate inflammaging through distinct molecular and cellular pathways. We examine the nocturnal dysregulation of the immune system, focusing on innate immune hyperactivation (e.g., via NLRP3 inflammasome and TLR4 signaling), cellular senescence (SASP), adaptive immune decline (T-cell aging), and disruption of systemic pathways such as the gut-brain axis. Clinical and epidemiological data link sleep disorders, particularly obstructive sleep apnea, to elevated inflammatory markers, accelerated epigenetic aging, and cognitive decline. Conversely, inflammaging impairs circadian regulatory structures, further degrading sleep quality. Interventions targeting the sleep-immune axis, including melatonin, circadian reinforcement, senotherapeutics, and lifestyle modifications, hold promise for mitigating inflammaging. We conclude that sleep disruption is not a passive symptom but an active driver of immunological aging, and propose that targeting this axis represents a viable strategy for promoting healthy longevity.

title: Tree Shrew as an Emerging Model for Aging Research: Characterization of Senescence and Therapeutic Interventions.
authors: Qiuni Luo; Wenxian Xiao; Xin Dong; Ayesha Nisar; Yuhua Ma; Xiang Lai; Raoxian Bai; Meiting Zi; Qi Geng; Qingyu Zhang; Cheng Zhang; Qiong Wang; Naheemat Modupeola Gold; Zhen Zhou; Li Hu; Ao Zhang; Qinghua Zeng; Jing Liu; Sawar Khan; Longbao Lv; Yonghan He
abstract: Aging is characterized by progressive physiological decline and increased susceptibility to age-related diseases. Conventional rodent models have contributed significantly to our understanding of aging, yet their translational relevance is limited by substantial evolutionary divergence from humans. Here, we introduce the tree shrew (Tupaia belangeri chinensis) as a novel and biologically relevant model organism for aging research. In vitro, we induced cellular senescence in tree shrew fibroblasts through ionizing radiation, doxorubicin treatment, or replicative exhaustion, all of which consistently triggered robust senescent phenotypes and a pronounced senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), accompanied by upregulation of conserved senescence biomarkers. In vivo, aged tree shrews exhibited progressive physical frailty, metabolic dysfunction, organ fibroplasia, and spontaneous tumorigenesis. Transcriptomic profiling uncovered widespread age-related alterations across multiple tissues, prominently affecting pathways involved in chronic inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and metabolic dysregulation. Further comparative transcriptomic analyses of liver and spleen tissues confirmed that tree shrews recapitulate conserved human aging transcriptional trajectories and core gene expression patterns, whereas mice displayed markedly divergent aging signatures. Notably, senolytic intervention with dasatinib and quercetin (D + Q) effectively reversed key transcriptional changes and ameliorated selected age-related pathologies, including hepatic steatosis. Importantly, the D + Q-induced transcriptomic responses in tree shrews exhibited markedly greater concordance with human aging signatures than did corresponding mouse datasets. Collectively, these findings establish the tree shrew as a translationally relevant aging model that bridges the gap between fundamental discovery and clinical application.

title: A Putative IL-17A-Senescence Feed-Forward Loop in Aging Skin.
authors: Dong Hun Lee; Yukie Yamaguchi

title: Senescent Mesenchymal Stromal Cells Drive Stem Cell Aging Through Dysregulated Chemokine Synthesis.
authors: Shaianne N Stein; Lorena R Braid
abstract: Aging is accompanied by a progressive decline in tissue regenerative capacity, driven by intrinsic stem cell dysfunction and age-associated deterioration of the surrounding stem cell niche. Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) are ubiquitous components of stem cell niches, where they integrate structural, metabolic, inflammatory, and paracrine cues to regulate stem cell quiescence, activation, and differentiation. With age, MSCs undergo functional decline and senescence, altering their secretory and signaling profiles. Across tissues, MSC senescence emerges as an intermediate amplifier of aging: molecular, metabolic, epigenetic, and inflammatory stressors promote the senescent state, which converts these upstream insults into chemokine imbalance, chronic inflammation, and progressive loss of stem cell support. Here, we synthesize classical and emerging literature to examine how age-associated changes in MSC chemokine synthesis contribute to stem cell aging, and we propose a synthesis-based model in which MSCs translate age-associated stressors into altered chemokine repertoires that disrupt stem cell-supportive signaling. We also discuss therapeutic strategies, including chemokine-directed therapies, senolytics, and MSC rejuvenation, that may restore regenerative capacity by normalizing MSC-derived signals. Together, the evidence identifies dysregulated chemokine synthesis as a conserved mechanism linking tissue-resident MSC aging to declining regenerative capacity.

title: Self-Reporting Hierarchical DNA Nanoplatform for Tumor Cell-Selective Senescence Modulation and Immune Remodeling.
authors: Wenya Dang; Jun Da; Jun Cao; Haolan Hu; Yuqi Xie; Lu Yu; Lu Wu; Linlin Wang; Jili Li; Yanlan Liu
abstract: Therapy-induced senescence (TIS) promotes tumor resistance and recurrence through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), but achieving tumor cell-selective senescence modulation remains a formidable challenge due to limited cellular specificity, insufficient spatiotemporal control, and the complexity of the secretory program. Here, we develop a self-reporting hierarchical DNA nanoplatform (Gal-lipo@S-CHA) that enables selective senescence reprogramming and immune remodeling in TIS tumor cells. In this design, a newly engineered β-galactosidase-responsive charge-reversal lipid carrier establishes the first layer of senescence selectivity by enabling preferential delivery and enhanced endosomal escape of a hierarchically gated catalytic DNA circuit. Subsequent intracellular decoding of GSH and microRNA-21, two tumor-associated and senescence-enriched molecular signatures, provides a second layer of tumor cell selectivity, activating the circuit specifically in pathological senescent tumor cells. The activated circuit simultaneously generates a fluorescence signal for real-time monitoring and assembles an NF-κB decoy to block NF-κB nuclear translocation, thereby suppressing downstream pro-tumorigenic SASP production at the upstream regulatory source. In vivo studies demonstrate that Gal-lipo@S-CHA effectively remodels the tumor immune microenvironment by enhancing natural killer cell infiltration and M1 macrophage polarization. Collectively, this framework establishes a new paradigm for selectively reprogramming pathological senescence, providing a versatile platform to support immunomodulatory cancer therapies.

title: Sunitinib induces senolysis associated with modulation of platelet-derived growth factor receptor beta.
authors: Hyun-Ji Cho; Sung Jin Ryu; Byung Ju Kim; Jeong-A Hwang; Ahyeon Yun; Eok-Cheon Kim; Jae-Ryong Kim; Tae Jun Park; Sung Bae Lee; Young Zoon Kim; Yun-Il Lee; Sang Chul Park; Young-Sam Lee
abstract: Receptor tyrosine kinases are critical regulators of cell survival, mediating responses to environmental changes and maintaining biological responsiveness. However, despite growing interest in developing senolytics that target survival factors in senescent cells as a promising strategy to overcome age-related diseases, the therapeutic potential of RTKs in senescence remains largely unexplored. In this study, we aimed to identify senolytic compounds that modulate RTK signaling and ameliorate age-related phenotypes by selectively inducing senescent cell death. Using a drug screening approach, we identified sunitinib, a multi-targeted RTK inhibitor that effectively suppresses PDGFR activation and induces apoptosis specifically in senescent HDFs (sHDFs) by activating caspase-9, -3, and -7. Moreover, in a mouse model of bleomycin-induced lung fibrosis in which senescent cells accumulate in the tissue, sunitinib reduced senescent cells and suppressed SASP expression. These findings, together with the observed increase in PDGFRβ phosphorylation in aged cells, led us to hypothesize that modulating PDGFRβ activity could induce senolysis. Indeed, knockdown of PDGFRβ expression sensitized senescent cells to cell death, with minimal effects on non-senescent HDFs (nsHDFs). At the mechanistic level, PDGFRβ and its downstream pathways, including the JAK2-STAT3 pathway, contributed to the senolytic response to sunitinib. Notably, sunitinib-induced JAK1 phosphorylation contributed to resistance to sunitinib in nsHDFs. Our findings suggest that sunitinib is a promising senolytic agent and that targeting PDGFRβ may represent a previously unknown approach to senolytics. Therefore, our study may provide a potential therapeutic strategy for age-related diseases associated with chronic inflammation.

title: Cellular senescence: six decades of discovery and reinvention.
authors: Myrthe Klaver; Lotte Sophie Steeneken; Naomi Veeningen; Abdullah Altulea; Marco Demaria
abstract: Cellular senescence has undergone a remarkable conceptual evolution since its discovery in 1961. Initially described by Hayflick and Moorhead as the finite proliferative lifespan of cultured human cells, senescence was first viewed as a consequence of cellular aging. The identification of telomere shortening, senescence biomarkers, and oncogene- and damage-induced senescence subsequently established its molecular basis and role as a tumor-suppressive stress response. The discovery of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) further transformed the field by revealing that senescent cells actively communicate with and remodel their tissue environment. Genetic mouse models later demonstrated causal roles for senescent cells in tissue repair, aging, and age-related disease, while senotherapeutics established senescence as a therapeutic target. Here, we trace the major conceptual transitions that shaped the field, from replicative endpoint to stress-response program, regulator of tissue homeostasis, driver of chronic pathology, and clinically actionable process. We discuss the discoveries, controversies, and technological advances underlying these transitions and how emerging single-cell technologies, precision biomarkers, and targeted interventions are shaping the next era of senescence research.

title: Senescence-associated prostate cancer cells promote fibroblast reprogramming and extracellular matrix remodeling.
authors: Chongsen Lin; Qianyu Guo; Shaohong Lai
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cellular senescence influences tumor progression via the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), yet whether senescence-associated alterations in prostate epithelial cells contribute to stromal remodeling remains poorly understood. METHODS: Human prostate cancer specimens, public single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets, a prostate-specific Pten conditional knockout (Pten-cKO) mouse model, mouse single-cell transcriptomic analysis, and mechanistic in vitro experiments were integrated to investigate senescence and stromal remodeling. Histopathological analysis, multiplex immunofluorescence staining, transcriptomic profiling, conditioned medium experiments, senolytic intervention, and pharmacological inhibition assays were employed to characterize epithelial-fibroblast interactions and their underlying mechanisms. RESULTS: Senescence-associated phenotypes were progressively enriched across increasing PCa grades and were predominantly localized to the epithelial compartment. Human single-cell transcriptomic analysis revealed concurrent activation of epithelial senescence/SASP programs and fibroblast ECM-remodeling programs, along with the enrichment of fibrogenic secretory signatures linked to epithelial-stromal communication. Consistently, Pten-cKO mouse prostates exhibited increased epithelial senescence-associated phenotypes, collagen deposition, and fibroblast ECM-remodeling activity. Mechanistically, DOX-induced senescence-associated RM1 prostate cancer cells acquired a fibrogenic secretory phenotype characterized by augmented TGF-β1 secretion. Senolytic treatment with ABT-263 reduced the senescence-associated cell population and TGF-β1 secretion, while conditioned medium collected after ABT-263 treatment exhibited diminished fibroblast-remodeling activity. DOX-RM1 conditioned medium reprogrammed NIH/3T3 fibroblasts into an ECM-remodeling CAF-like state, which was manifested by enhanced collagen deposition and upregulated expression of matrix-associated genes and proteins. Pharmacological inhibition of TGF-β signaling attenuated SMAD2 phosphorylation and partially reversed fibroblast activation and ECM remodeling. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify epithelial senescence-associated signaling as a mechanism linking prostate epithelial alterations to fibroblast reprogramming and ECM remodeling. A fibrogenic tumor-cell secretory program promotes fibroblast acquisition of an ECM-remodeling CAF-like phenotype, at least in part through TGF-β/SMAD2 signaling, and contributes to fibrotic remodeling of the prostate tumor microenvironment.

title: UHRF1 overexpression generates distinct senescent states with different Tp53 dependencies.
authors: Elena Magnani; Charlene Chen; Filippo Macchi; Tijana Randic; Bhavani P Madakashira; Ian McBain; Kirsten C Sadler
abstract: Senescence is a pleiotropic phenotype that alternatively suppresses or promotes cancer. Tumor-suppressive roles are attributed to irreversible cell cycle arrest and immune clearance, while tumor-promoting functions include apoptosis resistance and immune evasion, allowing cells to persist and support the tumor microenvironment or escape senescence and proliferate. Epigenetic changes are common features of senescent cells, and we used a preneoplastic liver cancer model caused by overexpression of the epigenetic regulator, UHRF1, in zebrafish hepatocytes to investigate how epigenome repatterning generates diverse senescent phenotypes. Early responses to UHRF1 overexpression include DNA damage, DNA methylome repatterning, retrotransposon derepression, cell cycle withdrawal, and atm and tp53-dependent senescence. scRNAseq analysis uncovers distinct senescent cell populations, some expressing immunogenic and anti-apoptotic genes, and others expressing proliferation genes. These populations have different capacities and susceptibilities based on UHRF1 levels. Cells with low UHRF1 levels proliferate in tp53 mutants, while cells with high UHRF1 levels do not re-enter the cell cycle and are targeted by the senolytic Navitoclax. This indicates that UHRF1 expression level can generate diverse senescent cell phenotypes with divergent outcomes.

title: Cellular senescence of fibro-adipogenic progenitors by STAT5A/GFPT2/O-GlcNAcylation impairs muscle recovery after glucocorticoid-induced injury.
authors: Bingfei Li; Wei Xiang; Wanwan Qi; Xinxin Liu; Weiwen Zhu; Wei Zhang; Runze Jin; Shuo Ma; Lifeng Chen; Chuanqing Bai; Shunzheng Fang; Jiangyi Wu; Xiaoqi Zhang; Limeng Dai; Xingying Guan; Jia Li; Song Li; Yan Xiong; Xiangqin Fang; Changyue Gao; Siru Zhou; Hong Guo; Zhenhong Ni
abstract: The clinical use of glucocorticoids often leads to skeletal muscle injury, characterized by muscle atrophy and dysfunction. Fibro-adipogenic progenitors (FAPs) play an important role in maintaining muscle homeostasis, but their roles in the recovery of skeletal muscle after glucocorticoid-induced injury remain largely elusive. Here, we reveal that glucocorticoid induces cellular senescence of FAPs, leading to their accumulation in skeletal muscle. Mechanistically, glucocorticoid enhances the expression of GFPT2 through STAT5A, which further elevates O-GlcNAcylation in FAPs and promotes their senescence. Targeting the STAT5A-GFPT2-mediated O-GlcNAcylation can reduce the burden of senescent FAPs in glucocorticoid-treated muscle and facilitate muscle recovery after injury. Our results demonstrate that exosomes derived from senescent FAPs suppress myotube formation, greatly inhibiting the regrowth of glucocorticoid-treated skeletal muscle. Moreover, senescent FAPs reduce the muscle stem cells (MuSCs) pool by suppressing their proliferation, thereby impairing the regenerative capacity of skeletal muscle during the recovery process after glucocorticoid treatment.

title: Cellular senescence as endocrine information failure in aging.
authors: Zheng Bi; Yixuan Lin
abstract: Endocrine organs translate nutrient, stress and circadian cues into hormone outputs that coordinate whole-body physiology. Cellular senescence can distort this communication by changing endocrine-cell identity, stimulus-secretion coupling, secretory timing and local immune or paracrine signaling. Evidence is strongest in pancreatic β-cells and the adrenal zona fasciculata, where composite senescence phenotypes have been linked to endocrine dysfunction and modified by targeted perturbations. β-cell senescence is not uniformly deleterious. Some states retain insulin production, support functional maturation or restrain immune injury, whereas others propagate inflammatory and paracrine dysfunction. Pituitary and thyroid findings support direct but narrower mechanisms, while parathyroid and pineal evidence remains largely downstream or axis level. No single marker identifies endocrine senescence across tissues, and therapeutic evidence remains predominantly preclinical. A state-resolved approach combining lineage localization, multiple senescence domains and dynamic endocrine readouts is needed to identify pathogenic states and evaluate intervention.

title: Mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites (MERCS/MAM): Multi-layered upstream regulators of microglial senescence in Alzheimer's disease.
authors: Annan Liu; Liping Xing; Jianhui Li; Wei Gao; Mingyuan Yao; Jing Song; Honglin Li
abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an age-dependent neurodegenerative syndrome in which microglial senescence bridges biological ageing and Aβ-tau pathology. Senescent microglia undergo permanent cell-cycle arrest, upregulate p16INK4a and SA-β-gal, and secrete a pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) that sustains chronic neuroinflammation. Mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites (MERCS) are dynamic physical junctions between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria, whereas mitochondria-associated membranes (MAM) are biochemically enriched ER subdomains located at MERCS. MERCS coordinate calcium shuttling, mitochondrial dynamics, lipid trafficking and the unfolded protein response (UPR); however, whether their dysfunction drives microglial senescence in vivo remains largely untested. MAIN TEXT: This review critically integrates five MERCS-linked signalling axes that are hypothesised to drive microglial senescence, namely calcium overload, mitochondrial fission-fusion imbalance, inflammatory amplification, lipid dysregulation and unresolved ER stress. We apply a standardized four-tier evidence-grading framework to stratify causal evidence, systematically distinguish dystrophic, disease-associated (DAM) and bona-fide senescent microglia on the basis of transcriptomic and proteomic data from AD models and human tissues, and address underexplored dimensions including APOE/TREM2 crosstalk, mitophagy, epigenetic regulation, peripheral inflammation and senolytic combinations. We stress that inflammatory activation, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction represent common cellular stress responses that cannot independently define bona-fide microglial senescence. Because more than 90% of current mechanistic evidence is derived from non-microglial models, MERCS dysfunction in microglia remains a compelling hypothesis that requires rigorous in-vivo validation. Notably, MERCS dysfunction and AD-relevant APOE/TREM2 signalling engage in mutually modulatory crosstalk rather than a simple linear upstream-downstream hierarchy. CONCLUSION: Translational development faces several barriers, including poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, off-target neurotoxicity, uncharacterised long-term safety and limited generalisability from APP/PS1 models lacking tauopathy. All MERCS-targeted and senolytic combinatorial strategies discussed herein represent prospective pre-clinical research directions rather than mature clinical therapeutic approaches. We propose an experimental roadmap based on conditional knockouts, intravital imaging and bidirectional interventions. Overall, MERCS dysfunction is proposed as a candidate multimodal upstream hub for calcium, mitochondrial, inflammatory, lipid and ER-stress signalling, and rigorous in-vivo validation together with microglia-selective delivery platforms is essential for therapeutic translation.

title: Intracranial aneurysms as a manifestation of premature vascular aging: Cellular senescence, inflammaging, and wall degeneration.
authors: Takuma Maeda; Hirotaka Sato; Yusuke Nakano; Hiroki Kobayashi; Yushiro Take; Peyton L Nisson; Oscar Cisneros; Redi Rahmani; Benjamin Jackson; Juliana C Castro; Misaki Tatsumi; Gia Patel; Evangeline L Little; Hannah Jackson; Michael T Lawton; Tomoki Hashimoto; Hiroki Sato
abstract: Aging is a major risk factor for the formation, growth, and rupture of intracranial aneurysms, but the underlying biological mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Beyond chronological aging, accumulating evidence suggests that vascular aging is driven by cellular senescence, chronic inflammation, and hemodynamic stress, which together contribute to aneurysm wall degeneration. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on the role of aging in intracranial aneurysm biology, with a particular focus on the interplay between senescent cells, inflammaging, and vascular remodeling. Senescent endothelial and smooth muscle cells exhibit a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), characterized by the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes, and oxidative stress mediators. These factors may contribute to extracellular matrix degradation, immune cell recruitment, and progressive weakening of the aneurysm wall. We also discuss the inconsistent association between age and aneurysm rupture across natural-history studies and the methodological factors that may contribute to this unresolved heterogeneity. Furthermore, we examine how aging-related alterations in vascular biology may modify the response to hemodynamic forces and therapeutic interventions. Finally, we explore emerging therapeutic strategies targeting aging pathways, including senolytics and senomorphics, as potential approaches for stabilizing aneurysms and preventing rupture. Understanding the mechanistic links between aging and aneurysm pathophysiology may open new avenues for risk stratification and disease-modifying treatments.

title: Exercise and p21 signaling in central nervous system aging and senescence: A context- and dose-dependent relationship.
authors: Chen Sun; Paramasivam Muthusamy; Ananthi Pattanimuthu; Muyuan Liu
abstract: Physical exercise is a potent modifier of CNS aging, but its relationship with the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21 (CDKN1A) is neither uniformly suppressive nor equivalent to cellular senescence. Direct evidence remains sparse and preclinical. Sustained physiological exercise reduced hippocampal or cortical p21-associated signatures in models of metabolic distress, natural aging, and amyloid pathology. Conversely, acute treadmill exercise transiently increased hippocampal Cdkn1a, while spatial transcriptomics identified increased endothelial Cdkn1a during broader exercise-associated vascular rejuvenation. At the maladaptive extreme, excessive swimming produced sustained hippocampal p53-p21 activation accompanied by oxidative injury, apoptosis, senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity, and cognitive impairment. Genetic studies further indicate that endogenous p21 restrains exercise-responsive neural stem-cell activation, but they do not demonstrate that exercise itself reduces p21. To reconcile these findings, this review applies a four-axis interpretive matrix based on signal persistence, cellular and subcellular compartment, corroborating senescence-associated features, and functional consequence. The evidence is integrated into three states: physiological exercise associated with attenuation of persistent p21-related stress, transient or cell-specific adaptive p21 induction, and maladaptive exercise overload characterized by sustained p53-p21 signaling and tissue injury. Current findings therefore support exercise more strongly as a stress-preventive or senomorphic intervention than as a proven CNS senolytic or p21-targeted therapy. The central question is not simply whether exercise increases or decreases p21, but when, where, for how long, and within which cellular and molecular context the response reflects repair, quiescence, persistent senescence-like dysfunction, or progression toward cell death.

title: Ruxolitinib preserves endothelial function in middle-aged and old mice after ischemia/reperfusion injury.
authors: Lars Saemann; Hatice Seda Soyer; Sabine Pohl; Saskia Hagewiesche; Leah Sarow; Sara Wambrauw; Merve Kuru-Schors; Andreas Simm
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Ischemia/Reperfusion (I/R) and the increasing age of patients are coexisting challenges in today's cardiovascular medicine. Vascular I/R leads to endothelial dysfunction and is partially driven by inflammation. With increasing age, a profile of biomolecules known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) also increases. The SASP correlates with decreased resilience and intrinsic capacity to withstand various stressors and contains pro-inflammatory cytokines, likely fueling I/R injury. Senomorphics block SASP secretion. We investigated the effect of ruxolitinib on endothelial function after vascular I/R injury in middle-aged and old mice. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Aortic rings of 11-13 and 23-25 months old C57BL/6 J mice were divided into three groups: Control (12 mo: n = 9; 24 mo: n = 10), ischemia/reperfusion (I/R group; 12 mo: n = 9; 24 mo: n = 11), and I/R with ruxolitinib (I/R + Ruxo; 12 mo: n = 13; 24 mo: n = 15). The aortic rings were stored in de-aired saline solution for 24 h without (I/R) or with ruxolitinib (I/R + Rux). Afterward, they were mounted in organ bath chambers. The reperfusion injury was induced by 200 μM sodium hypochlorite. In the Control group, no ischemia or sodium hypochlorite was performed. We investigated the vasomotor function using potassium chloride (KCl), phenylephrine (PE), acetylcholine (ACh), and sodium nitroprusside (SNP). RESULTS: The contraction to PE in % of KCl was higher in the I/R group (12 mo: 80 ± 10%; 24 mo: 94 ± 15%) compared to the control (12 mo: 51 ± 8%; 24 mo: 63 ± 13%) and lower in the I/R + Ruxo group (12 mo: 60 ± 9%; 24 mo: 70 ± 10%) compared to the I/R group, in both age populations. The maximal endothelial-dependent relaxation to ACh was substantially decreased in the I/R group (12 mo: 34 ± 6%; 24 mo: 34 ± 7%) compared to control (12 mo: 75 ± 5%; 24 mo: 88 ± 9%) and higher in the I/R + Ruxo group (12 mo: 59 ± 21%; 24 mo: 61 ± 12%) compared to I/R in both age populations. The endothelial-independent relaxation to SNP was comparable between all groups. The concentration of interleukin (IL)-1α, IL-7, IL-10, IL-13, and tumor necrosis factor-α was higher in the I/R + Ruxo group, only in 24-month-old mice. CC chemokine ligand (CCL)11, intercellular cell adhesion molecule-1, CCL8, RANTES, and C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 5 were comparable between I/R and I/R + Ruxo in 12- and 24-mo mice. CONCLUSION: Treatment of the aorta with the senomorphic agent ruxolitinib during ischemic storage protects the endothelial-dependent vasomotor function of the aorta in both age groups.

title: The senescence-immune axis as a target for combining immunotherapy and senotherapy.
authors: Fernanda Saez-Calazans; Lucas Kich Grun; Lucas Emanuel Stein; Florencia Barbé-Tuana; Eduardo Cremonese Filippi-Chiela
abstract: Cellular senescence and immune dysfunction intersect as central biological processes shaping disease progression and therapeutic responses across ageing-related pathologies. Rather than acting independently, senescent cells (SnCs) and immune cells engage in a dynamic and bidirectional crosstalk that influences immune surveillance, inflammatory signaling, and tissue remodeling. This review focuses on the molecular and cellular mechanisms through which SnCs modulate immune composition and function, emphasizing immune checkpoint ligands, stress-associated surface molecules, and senescence-associated transcriptional programs governing senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) expression. We further examine how immune-targeted therapies can, in turn, remodel senescent niches by promoting immune-mediated clearance or altering senescence-associated phenotypes. Integrating evidence from cancer to metabolic and chronic inflammatory diseases, we discuss how senotherapies reshape immune landscapes and how immunotherapies impact senescent cell burden and function. Building on these mechanistic insights, we propose that the senescence-immune axis constitutes a tractable therapeutic vulnerability that can be exploited through rational combination strategies. Finally, we outline five conceptual frameworks and biomarker-guided trial archetypes for integrating senotherapies and immunotherapies in a bidirectional crosstalk, aiming to enhance therapeutic efficacy while mitigating ageing- and treatment-associated toxicities. By reframing senescence and immunity as interconnected therapeutic targets, this review provides a mechanistic foundation for next-generation combinatorial interventions across ageing-associated diseases.

title: Cellular senescence in posterior segment neovascular diseases: A proposed feed-forward amplification model.
authors: Yumo Wang; Tianyi Luo; Cunzi Li; Lan Zhou; Hongzhan Lin; Ming-Ming Yang
abstract: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) and proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) continue to be significant contributors to permanent visual impairment. Although anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy has substantially improved disease management, recurrent neovascularization, persistent leakage, incomplete treatment response, subretinal fibrosis in nAMD, and fibrovascular membrane formation or tractional complications in PDR indicate that disease progression involves mechanisms beyond VEGF signaling alone. Cellular senescence-a stress-induced condition marked by persistent cell-cycle arrest, altered stress responses, and context-dependent senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) activity-has been identified as a potential pathogenic amplifier in posterior-segment neovascular diseases. Chronic oxidative stress, hyperglycemia, hypoxia, metabolic dysfunction, and inflammation in the retina and choroid may induce senescence-associated or senescence-like remodeling in retinal pigment epithelial cells, Müller glia, endothelial cells, and pericytes. Nonetheless, conclusive evidence of bona fide cellular senescence in human ocular tissues remains scarce and varies markedly across cell types and disease contexts. This review integrates direct experimental evidence, marker-based observations, and inferred mechanistic insights to delineate a proposed, evidence-based senescence-associated feed-forward amplification model. In this model, chronic pathological stress may initiate or reinforce senescence-related programs, whereas SASP factors, extracellular vesicles, and immune microenvironment remodeling may further amplify angiogenic, inflammatory, vascular, and fibrotic dysfunction. Importantly, this model should be interpreted as a hypothesis-generating, non-exclusive framework rather than a fully established causal pathway. We also compare disease-specific features of nAMD and PDR, discuss methodological challenges in defining retinal senescence, and evaluate the translational potential and safety concerns of senolytics and SASP-modulating strategies as adjuncts to anti-VEGF therapy. Rather than presenting cellular senescence as a fully established causal driver, this review frames senescence-associated remodeling as a context-dependent, evidence-stratified amplifying component within this proposed feed-forward framework.

title: Senescence of the immune system in SLE: Pathogenic mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
authors: Xiaojing Jiang; Ziqian Liang; Chaoran Zhao; Fang Li; Qinyi Su; Yan Wang; Shengxiao Zhang; Ting Cheng
abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a heterogeneous autoimmune disease characterized by loss of immune tolerance and multi-organ inflammation. Although its pathogenesis involves multiple factors, the peak incidence of SLE in individuals over 48 years of age points to immunosenescence as a key driver of the disease.Even in younger patients, SLE frequently often presents as premature aging of the immune system. This review synthesizes recent advances in understanding how immunosenescence drives pathogenesis through immune dysregulation across major lymphocyte and myeloid subsets. Within the chronic inflammatory microenvironment, replicative exhaustion of T cells leads to accelerated telomere attrition, persistent activation of the DNA damage response, and telomerase dysfunction. This cascade culminates in the accumulation of senescent T cells displaying a characteristic CD28-CD57+KLRG1+ phenotype, accompanied by a pro-inflammatory state defined by enhanced cytotoxicity and impaired regulatory function. These characteristics correlated directly with disease activity and cumulative organ damage. The process arises from the interplay of metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic remodeling. In parallel, age-associated B cells (ABCs) accumulate, producing high-affinity anti-dsDNA and other autoantibodies, and potentiating inflammation via enhanced antigen presentation. Meanwhile, an aged bone-marrow microenvironment together with clonal hematopoiesis skews monocyte and macrophage polarization toward a pro-inflammatory (M1) profile. These cells show reduced phagocytic capacity and heightened secretion of senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)-like mediators, further driving inflammaging. This review synthesizes current insights into the relationship between SLE risk and immunosenescence. We discuss the mechanisms through which immune aging instigates autoimmunity and explore emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at mitigating immunosenescence.

title: Exercise attenuates atherosclerosis by inhibiting eWAT aging via targeting SIRT1/pyruvate carboxylase pathway.
journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular basis of disease
authors: Meng Zhang; Mengyue Yang; Zhao Sun; Zhengwei Qiu; Ziyu Yang; Zhouhao Zhang; Yanchao Li; Xuedong Wang; Xingtao Huang; Qi Liu; Jingbo Hou; Bo Yu
abstract: Aging is the primary risk factor for atherosclerosis (AS). Epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT) is a key driver of organismal aging and age-related diseases. Exercise is known to protect against AS, but the role of aging eWAT in this process remains unclear. To this end, we investigated whether exercise inhibits AS by regulating aging eWAT and elucidated the involved mechanisms. ApoE-/- and C57BL/6 mice were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) to mimic poor lifestyle habits and explore eWAT senescence evolution. We found eWAT is a senescence-susceptible organ, exhibiting time-dependent deterioration under unhealthy lifestyle conditions. Furthermore, eWAT transplantation experiments confirmed that aging eWAT accelerates AS progression in both local and distal vascular regions. Exercise significantly ameliorated HFD-induced eWAT remodelling and inflammation, thereby inhibiting AS progression. Bioinformatics and lipidomic analyses identified that SIRT1 is essential for the anti-senescent eWAT effects of exercise by suppressing pyruvate carboxylase (PC). Contrarily, SIRT1 downregulation in eWAT with adeno-associated virus (AAV) reversed the exercise protective effects. Similarly, senolytic treatment (dasatinib plus quercetin) or PC downregulation with AAV also attenuated eWAT aging and AS progression. Our results demonstrate that exercise attenuates unhealthy lifestyle-induced premature aging of eWAT delays the progression of associated AS by modulating the SIRT1/PC axis. Thus, targeting this signaling axis may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for preventing AS and could serve as a potential alternative to exercise intervention.

title: Artemisinin and quercetin attenuate hydrogen peroxide-induced oxi-inflammatory-mitochondrial dysfunction-SASP axis mediated lung epithelial cell premature senescence via targeting Stat-1/Atm-p53/p16/p21/Bcl2, NOD-1/MAPKs/NF-κB/ signalling cascades.
authors: Suman Karadagatla; Hara Prasad Padhy; Anamika Sharma
abstract: The senescence of lung epithelial cells impairs self-repair and exacerbates lung damage in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The potential of natural phytochemicals to reverse premature senescence warrants investigation. Information regarding the independent multifaceted effect of quercetin and artemisinin on epithelial senescence has not been delineated yet. The present investigation aimed to comprehend their attributes on H2O2-induced hallmark of premature senescence via controlling the vicious circle of oxidative-inflammatory stress, impaired cell proliferation, apoptosis, DNA damage, and inflammatory senescence cascades. An in vitro model of H2O2-exposed BEAS-2B cells was used to explore senescence using microscopy, qRT-PCR, immunoblotting, flow cytometry, and NMR· H2O2 (100 µM) treatment induced cellular senescence-associated features without significant cytotoxicity, as evidenced by enhanced SA-β-galactosidase activity, irreversible irregular enlargement, shrinking, and flattened cell appearance, which was reversed by quercetin and artemisinin at varying degree. Results revealed that quercetin and artemisinin restored disrupted mitochondrial function in senescent cells, as evidenced by reduced MMP, GLS, ARRDC4, TXNIP, creatine, and increased NRF-2, HO-1, NQO-1, Sirt-1/5, and glycine levels. Furthermore, quercetin and artemisinin promoted proliferative ability, DNA repair, S-phase cell cycle transition, apoptosis, and suppressed SASP, as evidenced by enhanced Ki67 expression, annexin-V-positive cells, and diminished expression of interleukins, COX-2, MMPs, and the Atm/p53/p16/p21/Bcl-2 axis. Subsequently, activation of NOD-1, Stat-1, NF-κB, ERK1/2, p38, and JNK was decisively thwarted by quercetin and artemisinin. Intriguingly, Lamin B1 restoration and ROS inhibition were only noticed in quercetin, indicating both are effective in halting senescence through an alternative pathway. Overall, the present investigation emphasizes that quercetin and artemisinin exhibit both senolytic and senomorphic properties and could be valuable senotherapeutics for stress-induced premature senescence.

title: A photo-responsive, fisetin-functionalized DNA nanocage for programmed therapy to accelerate early-stage wound healing in aged skin.
authors: Ziqi Yue; Zhou Jiang; Yichen Yang; Wumeng Yin; Yunfeng Lin; Yang Gao; Xiaoxiao Cai
abstract: Age-related impaired wound healing presents distinct challenges compared to conventional wounds, primarily due to dysregulated phase kinetics of wound repair and chronic cellular senescence, which collectively disrupt the dynamic and orderly progression of tissue regeneration. Effective intervention requires a stage-specific and temporally programmed therapeutic strategy. To address this, we first performed transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq) to elucidate the differential healing trajectory between young and aged wounds. Herein, we construct a photo-responsive, Fisetin-functionalized DNA nanocage (TAF) for spatiotemporally precise therapy of aged wounds. TAF is composed of a tetrahedral DNA nanocage loaded with a miR-29-targeting antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) covalently linked through a photocleavable linker and noncovalently encapsulating the senolytic agent Fisetin. The TAF platform enables a programmed therapeutic strategy: (a) the intrinsic antioxidant capacity of DNA scavenges excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) during the early inflammatory phase; (b) photo-triggered ASO release in the proliferative phase promotes collagen synthesis; and (c) sustained Fisetin release eliminates senescent cells, fostering a pro-regenerative microenvironment. In vivo studies in aged mice reveal that TAF-mediated therapy significantly accelerates early wound closure and enhances high-quality tissue regeneration. In summary, TAF establishes an efficient nanomedicine platform that improves aged tissue repair through stage-specific, temporally programmed regulation.

title: Reprogramming the mitochondrial-circadian energy code with incretins.
journal: Trends in endocrinology and metabolism: TEM
authors: Enzo Nisoli; Maurizio Ragni; Chiara Ruocco; Alessandra Valerio
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction, circadian disruption, and the accumulation of senescent cells converge to impair metabolic flexibility, a unifying phenotype of obesity and aging. We frame obesity as a nutrient-driven and aging as a time-driven expression of a disrupted mitochondrial-circadian energy code, with shared outputs: impaired substrate switching and flattened energy rhythms. This opinion argues that restoring code integrity, indexed clinically by gains in metabolic flexibility, should guide therapy. Beyond appetite and glycemia, GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) and dual GLP-1/GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide) agonists may enhance mitochondrial efficiency, support circadian alignment, and temper prosenescent signaling across target tissues (muscle, liver, adipose, islets, and brain). We outline how node-specific and combination strategies (senolytics/senomorphics, mitophagy/NAD+ support, and chrono-entrainment) could reprogram systemic energy coordination, improve durability of response, and delay age-related metabolic decline.

title: Age and sex influence transcriptomic responses to statin therapy that control liver aging during systemic metabolic dysfunction.
authors: David S Umbaugh; Liuyang Wang; Kuo Du; Rajesh Kumar Dutta; Seh Hoon Oh; Georgia Sofia Karachaliou; Manal F Abdelmalek; Ayako Suzuki; Anna Mae Diehl
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Older age increases susceptibility to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), but whether it impacts response to therapies, and how the therapies impact regulators of biological aging, are poorly understood. Statins inhibit the mevalonate pathway to block cholesterol biosynthesis and are widely used in MASLD patients to reduce cardiovascular disease. Whether statins prevent progression to cirrhosis is under investigation. However, the molecular effects of statins in human liver, particularly in the context of aging, remain poorly defined. APPROACH AND RESULTS: We analyzed liver transcriptomes and matched clinical data from 368 adults enrolled in the Duke MASLD Biorepository with a focus on age-dependent responses and the interplay between senescence and ferroptosis, a regulated death process that is constrained by the mevalonate pathway. Serum ALT, AST, and LDL cholesterol levels were lower in statin users of both sexes, particularly among older individuals. Transcriptome analyses revealed that statin use is strongly associated with suppression of senescence-related pathways. Statin use is also associated with increased activation of pathways linked to ferroptosis. Both responses persisted after propensity score matching to control for clinical confounders and were validated in an independent obese cohort. CONCLUSIONS: Age-dependent transcriptional remodeling in the liver differs in statin users and non-users. Pathways involved in senescence are suppressed while those that promote ferroptosis are induced in statin users. These results suggest that statins may suppress biological aging in MASLD by acting as senolytics and highlight the complex, context-specific roles of senescence in liver adaptation and remodeling.

title: Intermittent hypobaric pressure induces selective senescent cell death and alleviates age-related osteoporosis.
authors: Bowen Meng; Yan Qu; Benyi Yang; Chaoran Fu; Yifan He; Jing Li; Rentao Wan; Xin Li; Zhulin Xue; Zeyuan Cao; Meng Hao; Xiao Zhang; Zhe An; Fen Chen; Ruibao Ren; Xueli Mao; Yang Cao; Songtao Shi
abstract: Senescent cell accumulation contributes to aging, and their clearance represents an effective anti-aging strategy. Current senolytic strategies focus on drug-mediated senescent cell clearance, but it is unknown whether a hypobaric condition can induce senescent cell death. Here we show that hypobaric pressure (HP) at -375 mmHg without hypoxia induces cells to undergo lysosome-dependent cell death (LDCD). Mechanistically, we unveil that HP activates transmembrane protein 59 (TMEM59) to induce cellular Ca2+ influx, which triggers calpain 2 to cleave lysosomal associated membrane protein 2 (LAMP2), leading to lysosomal membrane permeabilization and subsequent LDCD. Furthermore, given that senescent cells contain elevated numbers of lysosomes, we report intermittent HP treatment to specifically induce senescent cells to undergo LDCD and reduce the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. Eventually, we report that intermittent HP treatment can substantially extend the lifespan and rescue the osteoporosis phenotype in aged mice. This study reveals a previously unknown role of HP as a natural senolytic to eliminate senescent cells, and identifies TMEM59 as a new HP-activated ion channel protein.

title: SIRT3 deficiency triggers mitochondrial dysfunction-associated senescence to suppress colorectal cancer progression via SLC25A13 acetylation.
authors: Wei Liu; Hongyao Li; Xuelan Ma; Yi Wang; Yuanyuan Yang; Zhiqi Peng; Yingjie Wang; Jin Zhang; Bo Liu; Ning Li
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is frequently well-known to induce mitochondrial dysfunction-associated senescence (MIDAS), a specialized form of cellular senescence marked by a distinct senescent phenotype. Sirtuin-3 (SIRT3) is a key regulator of mitochondrial function through its deacetylase activity, and emerging evidence highlights that its deficiency induces MIDAS in fibroblasts. However, the precise mechanism by which SIRT3 regulates MIDAS, as well as the role of MIDAS in tumorigenesis, remains incompletely understood. Here, we report that SIRT3 deficiency inhibits colorectal cancer (CRC) progression by inducing MIDAS. Mechanistically, SIRT3 deacetylates the mitochondrial carrier SLC25A13 at lysine 568. SIRT3 loss triggers K568 hyperacetylation, impairing SLC25A13 function and disrupting the malate-aspartate shuttle. This cascade reduces the cytosolic NAD+/NADH ratio, activating the AMPK-p53 axis to initiate MIDAS. Clinically, low levels of SLC25A13-K568 acetylation are associated with poor prognosis in human CRC. Furthermore, senolytic treatment selectively eliminates these senescent cells and suppresses tumor growth. Our findings unveil a SIRT3-SLC25A13 axis governing NAD+/NADH homeostasis and MIDAS, revealing a potential therapeutic strategy for CRC.

title: A three-hit sequential model of chemo-brain: from peripheral inflammation to central oxidative stress and synaptic dysfunction.
authors: Hui Yang; Yue Su; Yuying Zhong; Kehui Yang; Kaihui Shen; Xiaolan Cheng
abstract: BACKGROUND: Chemotherapy-induced central neurotoxicity (CICN), commonly known as "chemo-brain", is a prevalent and debilitating condition in cancer survivors, characterized by persistent cognitive deficits that severely compromise quality of life. Despite extensive research, the pathophysiology of CICN remains fragmented, lacking a unifying model that explains how it progresses from peripheral insult to chronic cognitive consolidation. AIM OF REVIEW: This review proposes a novel Three-Hit sequential model to reconceptualize CICN as a dynamic, staged pathological continuum. Unlike existing multi-hit hypotheses that largely describe cumulative or concurrent CNS risk factors, the Three-Hit model features a therapy-triggered, outside-in cascade with defined temporal checkpoints. The model aims to unify disparate mechanistic findings, explain the enduring nature of cognitive deficits after treatment cessation, and guide stage-specific, mechanism-based precision interventions. KEY SCIENTIFIC CONCEPTS OF REVIEW: The model delineates three sequential pathological phases. The First Hit (peripheral priming) involves chemotherapy-induced gut dysbiosis and systemic inflammation. The Second Hit (central amplification) entails blood-brain barrier disruption, microglial activation, and oxidative stress-driven synaptic dysfunction. The Third Hit (network consolidation) is defined by epigenetic reprogramming, cellular senescence, and white matter degradation, which collectively solidify chronic cognitive impairment. This staged model may facilitate the design of phase-targeted interventions, including microbiota modulation (First Hit), anti-inflammatory and BBB-stabilizing agents (Second Hit), and senotherapeutics or HDAC6 inhibitors (Third Hit), and may guide neuroprotective strategies toward better-timed application. By linking mechanistic insights to a staged biomarker ecosystem, this review offers a conceptual roadmap for advancing stage-specific therapies for CICN.

title: Immunosenescence remodels the osteoimmune microenvironment in osteoarthritis: from cellular crosstalk to regenerative therapeutics.
authors: Ruofan Liu; Ziheng Zhu; Yunfei Li; Xiaoman Xing; Xinyang Wang; Chuanbing Huang
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) has evolved from a condition conventionally regarded as mere mechanical "wear and tear" to a complex, whole-joint disorder driven by chronic low-grade inflammation and cellular dysfunction. Within the joint, the osteoimmune microenvironment-composed of articular cartilage, synovium, subchondral bone, the infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP), and resident stem cell niches-serves as the central site of osteoimmune interaction for maintaining tissue homeostasis and repair. Accumulating evidence indicates that age-associated dysregulation and senescence of innate and adaptive immune cell subsets represent major contributors to OA progression. Age- and senescence-associated immune states generate persistent inflammatory, oxidative, and damage-associated signals that contribute to microenvironmental deterioration. In this review, we propose a unified framework elucidating how immunosenescence reshapes the osteoimmune microenvironment via aberrant intercellular communication. We systematically delineate the distinct cellular crosstalk networks connecting immunosenescent drivers with chondrocytes, synovial fibroblasts, subchondral bone remodeling units, IPFP adipocytes, and mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs). Furthermore, we highlight emerging therapeutic avenues to reprogram this senescent niche, encompassing senotherapeutics, immunometabolic reprogramming, biomaterial-assisted targeted delivery, and engineered cell therapies. Finally, we propose the "Resolution Failure Hypothesis" as a testable mechanistic framework in which impaired efferocytosis and dysregulated specialized pro-resolving mediator (SPM) signaling may contribute to the persistence of osteoimmune remodeling. Rather than proposing defective inflammation resolution as a new biological phenomenon, this framework integrates established resolution-related mechanisms with age-associated immune remodeling and asks whether insufficient restoration of clearance and resolution capacity helps explain the incomplete structural recovery observed after senescent-cell-targeted interventions. Reconceptualizing OA through the lens of immunosenescent crosstalk will accelerate the translation of disease-modifying therapies from microenvironmental modulation toward functional joint regeneration.

title: Cellular senescence in skin inflammation: molecular mechanisms and potential clinical implications.
authors: Xinhe Wang; Beibei Xiong; Shuxiao Li; Yi Wang; Fulun Li
abstract: Cellular senescence is increasingly regarded as a mechanism linking chronic tissue stress to persistent skin inflammation. Senescent cells are defined by stable cell-cycle arrest with remodeling of morphology, metabolism, and secretory phenotype, of which the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) is central. Because no single marker is sufficient, senescence in skin requires multiparameter, cell-type-resolved criteria. This Review addresses stress sensing, SASP induction, paracrine propagation, immune evasion, cellular heterogeneity, and therapeutic targeting, stratifying evidence by disease: chronic and diabetic wounds are best supported, whereas in psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, cutaneous lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, and vitiligo the evidence remains largely associative, as SASP-like mediators overlap with cytokine programs from activated keratinocytes, stromal cells, and immune cells. Senescence-targeted interventions are classified as senolytics, senomorphics, or senopreventive/geroprotective strategies, and assessed at marker, SASP, senescent-cell-burden, and disease-outcome levels. It further notes that clinical translation depends on defining senescence-maintained lesion subtypes, establishing combinatorial biomarkers and spatial maps, and validating the efficacy and safety window of local therapies in suitable models and human tissues.

title: Recognizing senescent vascular smooth muscle cells in diabetic atherosclerosis: biomarkers, transcriptomic signatures, and methodological validity.
authors: Xiaoxu Yang; Di Zhao
abstract: Diabetic atherosclerosis represents the most severe macrovascular complication of diabetes mellitus and a major contributor to global morbidity and mortality. Senescence of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) has been increasingly recognized as a central mechanism driving plaque formation, progression, and instability under diabetic conditions. Yet identifying senescent VSMCs reliably remains difficult: available biomarkers lack specificity, transcriptomic signatures vary considerably across studies, and no consensus has emerged on how senescence should be verified methodologically. This review consolidates current knowledge on senescent VSMC identification in diabetic atherosclerosis. We begin with the pathobiological routes through which hyperglycemia drives VSMC senescence, including oxidative stress, DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and metabolic reprogramming. We then present a multidimensional classification of senescence-associated biomarkers, spanning cell cycle regulators, senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal), telomere-related markers, the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), calcification markers, and emerging non-coding RNA signatures, and assess the applicability and shortcomings of each. Transcriptomic signatures derived from single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and flow cytometry are then integrated to map the heterogeneity of senescent VSMC subpopulations and their functional roles within atherosclerotic plaques. We next appraise the methodological validity of existing detection strategies, comparing in vitro high-glucose models, in vivo diabetic animal models, and clinical specimens, and trace the sources of inter-study inconsistency, including spatial heterogeneity, cross-sectional designs, and the absence of standardized protocols. Finally, we outline a stepwise identification pipeline extending from molecular markers to functional validation and multi-omics integration, and consider future prospects such as senolytic therapies and targeted delivery systems. By providing this methodological reference, we hope to support both basic research and clinical translation and to push the field toward more precise, standardized identification of senescent VSMCs.

title: Senotherapeutics for Age-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders: A Systematic Review of Preclinical Evidence.
authors: Angela Falvino; Roberto Bonanni; Calogero Asaro; Pierangelo Cifelli; Umberto Tarantino; Elena Gasbarra; Virginia Tancredi; Ida Cariati
abstract: Aging is an important risk factor for musculoskeletal disorders such as osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, and sarcopenia. Cellular senescence contributes to age-related tissue deterioration by promoting functional alterations and a pro-inflammatory environment, making senotherapeutics promising strategies to selectively eliminate senescent cells or limit their deleterious effects. Our systematic review synthesized the available preclinical evidence on the efficacy of senotherapeutics in murine models of osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, and sarcopenia, analyzing structural and functional outcomes and the main molecular mechanisms involved in the regulation of cellular senescence. A literature search was conducted in the MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science databases according to PRISMA guidelines, while the methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the SYRCLE RoB tool. 26 experimental studies were included, of which 15 involved osteoarthritis models, 6 osteoporosis models, and 5 sarcopenic models. Overall, senotherapeutics demonstrated protective effects on musculoskeletal tissues by reducing inflammation and improving the evaluated outcomes through the modulation of pathways associated with cellular senescence. However, the heterogeneity of experimental models, therapeutic protocols, and outcome measures limits the possibility of drawing definitive conclusions. Further studies will be necessary to clarify the molecular mechanisms involved, optimize therapeutic strategies, and promote the translation of experimental evidence into clinical practice.

title: Cellular senescence in calcific aortic valve disease: are we ready for senolytic therapy?
authors: Ludovica Simonini; Ilenia Foffa; Augusto Esposito; Cecilia Vecoli
abstract: Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) is the most prevalent valvular heart disease in the Western countries and carries significant morbidity and mortality, yet no pharmacological therapy has demonstrated efficacy in modifying its natural history. Once regarded as a passive degenerative process, CAVD is now recognized as an actively regulated disease driven by endothelial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, dysregulated mineral metabolism, and cellular senescence, which collectively drive progressive fibrotic remodeling and calcification of the valve leaflets through both dystrophic and osteogenic mechanisms. This review examines the pharmacological strategies that have been investigated or are currently under evaluation to slow CAVD progression, encompassing lipid-lowering agents, renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, bone resorption inhibitors, vitamin K supplementation, and nitric oxide pathway modulators. Despite strong biological rationale and encouraging observational or preclinical data, each of these approaches has thus far failed to demonstrate consistent disease, modifying efficacy in prospective randomized trials, reflecting the complexity of CAVD pathophysiology and the historical lack of mechanistic precision in patient selection and trial design. Emerging evidence suggests that cellular senescence may represent a unifying and potentially actionable therapeutic target, bridging endothelial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and active calcification within a single pathophysiological framework. Preclinical studies demonstrate that senolytic clearance of senescent cells reduces calcification in atherosclerosic and hypercholesterolemic vascular models provide a compelling rationale for extending this approach to valvular targets.

title: Immunotherapy targeting an endogenous retrovirus decreases islet senescence markers and preserves glucose control in a mouse model of type 2 diabetes.
authors: Daniel Bjørklund Andersen; Nanna Skeltved; Gabriel Mira González; Thomas Garde-Due; Iker Ausina; Clara Iacumin; Lasse Neukirch; Anne-Marie Andersson; Emeline Ragonnaud; Joachim Størling; Claus Desler; Frederik Otzen Bagger; Kaare Villum Grunddal; Peter Johannes Holst
abstract: Type 2 diabetes is characterized by progressive metabolic stress and accumulation of senescent cells in key metabolic tissues, such as the pancreas, adipose tissue, and liver. Cellular senescence - an irreversible growth-arrested, and pro-inflammatory cell state can lead to induction of endogenous retrovirus (ERV) expression, which can also trigger cellular senescence. This possibly implies that a self-reinforcing ERV-senescence axis contributes to the metabolic decline and T2D. Here we developed and tested a mouse endogenous retrovirus (muERV) based active immunotherapy targeted at the most intact muERV, IAPE (Intracisternal A-type Particles elements with an Envelope) to eliminate cells expressing muERVs and senescence-associated proteins in a mouse model of accelerated diabetes combining a high-fat diet (HFD) with dexamethasone (DEX) and streptozotocin (STZ) (DS-HFD). Immunized DS-HFD mice (DS-HFD + IAPE-Tx) showed increased B and T cell responses towards IAPE. Antisera generated using our IAPE-targeted active immunotherapy was used to confirm activation of IAPE expression in the murine β-cell line MIN-6, following both inflammatory (cytokines) and chemical stress (STZ and DEX). In vivo, DS-HFD + IAPE-Tx mice showed reduced weight gain, improved fasting insulin-glucose homeostasis and oral glucose tolerance. They furthermore showed reduction in histomorphometry features consistent with steatosis, hepatocyte binucleation, reduced adipocyte size, and pancreatic islet senescence markers p16INK4a and p21Cip1/waf1, with a slight decrease in islet IAPE. Finally, we show activation of a human orthologue to IAPE, HERV-K, in cytokine-exposed isolated human pancreatic islets and EndoC-βH5 β-cells. Together, our results suggest that ERV antigens are expressed in metabolic disease models and may be targeted by immunotherapy to improve metabolic parameters, through a potential senolytic or senostatic-related but so far undefined mechanism.
