title: Standard treatment against paediatric BRAF-V600E glioma promotes senescence and sensitizes tumours to BCL-xL inhibition.
authors: Romain Guiho; Hiba Hamdi; Grace Cooksley; Timoty H Chang; Lei Cao; Romain Sigaud; Sophie Bliss; Ashley Vardon; Scott Haston; Florian Selt; Akang Leonard Bassey; Daniela Kocher; Ria Kedia; Daniel Gharai; Jesús Gil; Olaf Witt; Till Milde; Darren Hargrave; Paula Alexandre; Pratiti Bandopadhayay; Juan Pedro Martinez Barbera
abstract: BACKGROUND: Chemo-, radio-, and targeted therapies can induce a stable growth arrest known as therapy-induced senescence (TIS), which may be therapeutically exploited using senolytic compounds that selectively eliminate senescent cells. Children with BRAF-V600E-driven brain tumours are commonly treated with low-dose chemotherapies and MAPK inhibitors, alone or in combination, often with good initial responses. However, a majority of patients experiences tumour regrowth following treatment withdrawal. Here, we investigate the contribution of TIS to treatment response and relapse, and assess the therapeutic potential of senolytics in preclinical models of paediatric BRAF-V600E glioma. METHODS: Preclinical models of paediatric low-grade glioma were analysed in vitro or following orthotopic transplantation into mice and treated with Dabrafenib, Trametinib, Tovorafenib or Vinblastine. Senescence was assessed using molecular and cytological markers. Sensitivity to senolytic compounds was evaluated using in vitro dose-response assays and in vivo treatment studies. RESULTS: Trametinib induced a robust senescent phenotype in BT-40 tumours in vivo, characterised by activation of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype and expansion of IBA-1-positive myeloid cells. In vitro, senescence was induced in BT-40 cells following treatment with MAPK inhibitors and Vinblastine, and was similarly observed in H9-derived human neural stem cells expressing BRAF-V600E. Navitoclax was identified as a potent senolytic against senescent BT-40 cells, primarily through inhibition of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-xL. In vivo, combined Trametinib and Navitoclax treatment ablated senescent tumour cells, significantly reduced tumour regrowth after treatment withdrawal, and improved survival. CONCLUSIONS: These findings demonstrate that Navitoclax enhances Trametinib's anti-tumour efficacy and limits tumour relapse following treatment cessation.

title: Immunosenescence and Inflammaging in the Pathogenesis of Non-Melanoma Skin Cancer.
authors: Martina Mihalj; Nika Filipović Mioč; Iva Sabljić; Zdenka Šitum Čeprnja; Stana Tokić; Marija Buljan
abstract: Non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC) is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy worldwide, and its incidence rises disproportionately with age. While cumulative ultraviolet (UV) exposure is the dominant recognised risk factor, it does not fully account for the steep age-associated increase in NMSC, suggesting that additional, underrecognised mechanisms operate in older skin. This review synthesises evidence that immune senescence (the age-related remodelling of innate and adaptive immunity) is a central and partly modifiable driver of NMSC aetiopathogenesis. We first outline the classical risk factors and the epidemiological and economic burden of NMSC, and revisit the proposal to regard recurrent NMSC as a chronic disease. We then examine four interlocking, age-associated processes: the accumulation of senescent cells and their pro-inflammatory secretory phenotype ("inflammaging") in the skin microenvironment; UV-induced suppression of cutaneous immune function; age-related dysbiosis of the skin microbiome and its impact on antitumour immunity; and the systemic decline of T-cell-mediated tumour immunosurveillance. We integrate these processes into a framework in which immune senescence contributes to the progression of accumulated cutaneous damage to overt malignancy, and consider the implications for prevention (including senotherapeutics, microbiome modulation, and immune-stratified surveillance) that extend beyond UV-directed measures alone.

title: Improved preservation of hearts from old donors during static cold storage by the senomorphic agent ruxolitinib.
authors: Lars Saemann; Belma Kozar; Sabine Pohl; Anna Hoffmeister; Lena Wernstedt; Yao Gong; Andreas Simm; Gábor Szabó
abstract: PURPOSE: Hearts from old donors are more likely to develop primary graft dysfunction, presumably due to reduced tolerance to ischemia/reperfusion injury, partially driven by proinflammatory cytokines. Accumulating senescent cells secrete the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), including proinflammatory cytokines, potentially intensifying IRI. Senomorphic agents block the SASP. We investigated the effect of the senomorphic agent ruxolitinib on the contractility of hearts from old donors. METHODS: We procured hearts from 24-month-old male and female C57BL6/J mice and preserved them by static cold storage (SCS) for 2 h using histidine-tryptophan-ketoglutarate (HTK) solution, without or with ruxolitinib (HTK + Ruxo), and measured contractility before and after SCS. In the Control group, hearts were not preserved by SCS (N = 5 per Group and sex). We determined SASP-related cytokine release after SCS, JAK pathway, and nitrotyrosine levels. RESULTS: Especially in hearts from female mice (developed pressure, DP: 111 ± 17 vs. 44 ± 10%, p < 0.05) and (minimal slope of pressure decrement, dp/dtmin: 103 ± 13 vs. 78 ± 8%), but also in hearts from male mice, the ventricular function (DP, 71 ± 9% vs. 47 ± 18%; dp/dtmin, 87 ± 7% vs. 54 ± 10%) was higher in the HTK + Ruxo vs. the HTK group. IL-1α, IL-7, and nitrotyrosine levels were lower in the HTK-Ruxo group, independent of sex, and TNFα was lower only in the hearts of female mice. The phosphorylation of JAK2 was increased in the hearts of male mice in the HTK group. CONCLUSION: The senomorphic agent ruxolitinib improves contractility and modifies the SASP-related cytokine release during SCS of hearts from old donors in mice and is more effective in female hearts.

title: A Bi-Adjuvant Senolytic Nanovaccine Modulating Dendritic Cell Senescence Ameliorates Aging-Related Metabolic Dysfunction.
authors: Qingxu Song; Xiaoxue Du; Wenbo Dong; Ying Wang; Xiaojing Wang; Qiliang Yin
abstract: Senolytic vaccines hold promise for eliminating senescent cells, but their efficacy is limited by poor seno-antigen immunogenicity and age-related dendritic cell (DC) dysfunction. Here, we engineered an active biomaterial-enabled bi-adjuvant senolytic nanovaccine (CK5-GC-NV) by co-assembling CpG oligodeoxynucleotide with a fusion protein of the seno-antigen Gpnmb and a cationic spider silk protein variant (CK5). Beyond antigen delivery, the CK5 scaffold acts as an intrinsic senomodulator associated with the downregulation of mitotic kinases Aurka/b and a concomitant decrease in senescence-associated PI3K/AKT phosphorylation in DCs. This intervention attenuates aged DC phenotypes, restores antigen cross-presentation, and synergizes with CpG to elicit potent cytotoxic T-lymphocyte responses against senescent targets. Across multiple aging mouse models, CK5-GC-NV immunization orchestrated targeted clearance of Gpnmb+ senescent adipocytes, profoundly ameliorating metabolic dysfunction and extending lifespan. This multifunctional biomaterial platform integrates seno-antigen immunogenicity enhancement with the restoration of aged DC function, providing a promising proof-of-concept for antigen-directed gerotherapeutics.

title: From telomere dysfunction to seno-antigen selection: a conceptual framework and route-specific evidence appraisal for senolytic immunotherapy.
authors: Sarfaraz K Niazi
abstract: Cellular senescence causally contributes to age-related and chronic diseases, rendering the targeted immune clearance of pathological senescent cells a promising therapeutic avenue. Progress remains limited by heterogeneity across cell lineages, tissues, inducing stressors, and temporal factors. As antigen expression alone does not ensure immune accessibility, functional recognition, or safety for healthy tissues, these aspects warrant thorough evaluation. A conceptual framework is proposed, distinct from a validated or implementable algorithm, for identifying and prioritizing senescence-associated antigens. This framework requires four criteria that a single candidate antigen must meet within the same cellular context: persistent pathological senescence, immune accessibility via a confirmed surface antigen or naturally presented human leukocyte antigen (HLA) peptide, modality-appropriate functional immune recognition, and exclusion from vital healthy or beneficially senescent states. The mechanistic origin, such as telomere dysfunction, serves as an optional stratification axis that defines coherent subsets rather than a universal prerequisite; data lacking matched telomere and antigen information in the same cells remain unverified. The process distinguishes target nomination from product validation: evidence of recognition in a single modality, such as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) targeting of a surface antigen, does not confirm validation for alternatives like peptide vaccines. Application of the framework to urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor (uPAR) and glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein B (GPNMB) indicates that neither candidate currently meets all criteria, and the telomere axis remains untested for both. Given that multivalent vaccination elicits immunity against each component independently, combining candidates that fail individual criteria risks amplifying liabilities rather than ensuring intersectional specificity. This outcome would require an engineered AND-gated recognition system, where the capitalized operators AND, OR, and NOT denote Boolean logic gates rather than emphasis. The framework remains in the validation phase. Each criterion receives an ordinal grade, a non-compensatory decision rule, a route-specific ligand-density window that sets the quantitative condition for recognition and healthy-cell sparing, and a predefined seven-compartment counter-screening panel. Recognition architectures are formally compared, and a pre-registered benchmarking study with specified falsification criteria is outlined as the framework's validation test.

title: The aging secretome as a candidate driver of bone remodeling imbalance: myokines, adipokines, and senescence-associated secretory factors.
authors: Hanhong Fang; Xianglong Zhou; Yang Liu; Weicheng Chen; Fulin Zhou; Haoran Zhou; Jianhui Xiang; Liming Xiong
abstract: Bone homeostasis depends on the spatial and temporal coupling of osteoclastic resorption to osteoblastic formation. With aging, this balance shifts toward net bone loss alongside sarcopenia, marrow adipose expansion, and chronic low-grade inflammation. These parallel changes may be linked by a shared set of secreted signals, termed here the aging secretome. We distinguish functional remodeling imbalance, defined as a sustained shift between formation and resorption, from direct uncoupling, in which a resorption-to-formation coupling signal is demonstrably disrupted. The aging secretome comprises three principal arms: muscle-derived signals, including myostatin, irisin, and myogenic extracellular vesicles; fat-derived signals, including leptin, adiponectin, and marrow adipocyte lipotoxicity; and senescence-associated secretory factors, particularly those involving senescent osteocytes, TNF-α, and IL-6. Inflammaging is treated as a shared contextual amplifier rather than a separate signaling arm. These pathways converge on key regulators of skeletal remodeling, including RANKL, Wnt-sclerostin, and IGF-1. This framework also provides a common context for comparing pathway-specific interventions, such as activin type II receptor blockade and sclerostin inhibition, with broader approaches targeting senescence or inflammation. An early phase 2 senolytic trial was negative overall, with only an exploratory signal in women with high senescent-cell burden. The aging secretome should therefore be viewed as an organizing framework whose individual pathways and relative contributions require further validation in human bone.

title: Reshaping the tumor immune microenvironment via therapy-induced senescence: senescence-associated secretory phenotype networks and senolytic strategies.
authors: Xiaonan Geng; Peide Li; Ke Xu; Shuwen Yang; Xinjun Hu
abstract: Anticancer therapy can suppress tumor growth by inducing cell death, but many treatments also impose durable stress programs in malignant and stromal cells. Therapy-induced senescence (TIS) has emerged as a central non-lethal outcome of chemotherapy, radiotherapy and targeted therapy. Senescent cells remain metabolically active and communicate with their surroundings through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), a heterogeneous mixture of cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, proteases, extracellular vesicles and immune-modulatory signals. In cancer, this secretory program can support immune surveillance when it is transient and efficiently cleared, yet it can also promote chronic inflammation, immune suppression, stromal remodeling, recurrence and resistance when senescent cells persist. This review summarizes the TIS-SASP-tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) axis, with emphasis on the molecular regulation of SASP, immune-cell-specific remodeling, the biphasic nature of SASP-mediated immunity and the rationale for sequential senogenic-senolytic therapy. Here, "senogenic" refers to interventions that induce cellular senescence, "senolytic" to approaches that selectively eliminate senescent cells, and "senomorphic" to strategies that suppress or remodel harmful senescence-associated phenotypes without necessarily killing senescent cells. We discuss how senolytics, senomorphics and immune checkpoint combinations may convert therapy-induced senescence from a liability into a therapeutically exploitable state. We also highlight the translational barriers that currently limit this strategy, including biomarker specificity, cell-type heterogeneity, treatment timing, safety and the need for spatially resolved monitoring of senescent niches.

title: A Senescence-Driven Fibroblast-Macrophage Feed-Forward Circuit Promotes Radiation-Induced Cutaneous Fibrosis.
journal: International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics
authors: Eun Joo Chung; Santwana Kc; Seokjoo Kwon; Ayla White; Joon-Yong Chung; Youngjoo Jung; Heesu Ahn; Hong Zhang; Edmund Cauley; Deborah E Citrin
abstract: PURPOSE: Therapeutic radiation for superficial tumors may cause cutaneous fibrosis, a late side effect with limited treatment options. Here, we investigated the underlying mechanisms driving radiation-induced cutaneous fibrosis. METHODS AND MATERIALS: C3H/HeN mice received 35 Gy unilateral hindlimb irradiation. Cutaneous tissues from irradiated and contralateral unirradiated legs were analyzed by spatial whole transcriptome profiling using the GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiler platform. Beginning 5 weeks after IR, mice received the senolytic agent ABT-263 (50 mg/kg/d) or vehicle (n ≥ 10/group) by oral gavage (5 consecutive days followed by a 2-week rest for 3 cycles). Hindlimb contracture was assessed at 150 days after IR. Senescence and macrophage markers were evaluated by immunohistochemistry and quantitative PCR. Cellular senescence and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors were evaluated in irradiated fibroblasts and their culture media using senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity assays and multiplex immunoassays. The senolytic activity of ABT-263 in irradiated primary fibroblasts and effects of ABT-263 on primary macrophage cultures were evaluated in vitro. RESULTS: Spatial whole-transcriptomic analysis of irradiated murine dermis identified expression patterns consistent with macrophage activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and a SASP-rich environment. In vitro studies identified that the irradiated fibroblast-derived SASP induced a senescent phenotype in unirradiated fibroblasts and macrophages. SASP-induced senescent-like macrophages acquired a CD206+ profibrotic phenotype and, in concert with activated fibroblasts, initiated a feed-forward loop amplifying IL-6 and collagen production. SASP exposure increased expression of Bcl-2 family proteins in macrophages and fibroblasts, rendering both populations susceptible to clearance by the senolytic agent ABT-263. In vivo, ABT-263 effectively mitigated radiation-induced dermal fibrosis, depleted senescent fibroblasts and CD206⁺ macrophages, and reduced IL-6 expression. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings identify senescence-driven reciprocal macrophage-fibroblast interactions as key mediators of cutaneous fibrosis and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of senolytic interventions for treating late radiation-induced skin injury.

title: The Immune-Senescent Switch in Oral Carcinogenesis: From Premalignancy to Malignant Transformation-Does Periodontitis Tip the Balance? A Hypothesis-Driven Review.
authors: Shujing Lyu; Eva González-Angulo
abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) accounts for approximately 90% of oral malignancies, and most cases arise from oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) against a background of chronic inflammation. Periodontitis, a highly prevalent chronic inflammatory disease, is increasingly implicated as a risk factor for OSCC, yet the mechanistic link between these conditions remains unclear. This review proposes that immunosenescence-the age-related decline in immune function-may provide this link. We synthesise evidence indicating that periodontitis promotes immune ageing in oral and systemic immune compartments, encompassing T-cell exhaustion, the accumulation of senescent immune cells, and a pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP); together, these changes progressively weaken local immunosurveillance. On this basis, we introduce the "immune-senescent switch" as a conceptual framework-explicitly distinguished from established evidence-in which senescence is hypothesised to initially act as a tumour-suppressive barrier in early OPMDs but to be converted into a tumour-promoting force by chronic, periodontitis-driven immunosenescence. We critically evaluate the supporting evidence, including the single-arm phase 2 COIS-01 trial (n = 24), in which senolytics combined with anti-PD-1 therapy achieved a 33.3% major pathological response rate in resectable head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, while emphasising the preliminary, hypothesis-generating nature of these data. Finally, we discuss emerging senotherapeutic strategies, translational gaps, and future research priorities.

title: Olfactory Receptor 51E2 Activation by β-Ionone Induces a Senescence-Like Phenotype and Increases Susceptibility to Senolytic Treatment in Colorectal Cancer.
authors: Ji-Sun Kim; Jin-A Kim; Young Hun Jung; Jung-Won Choi; Sung Won Shin; Byeongkyu Kang; Byung Soh Min; Hunsang Lee; Seok Chung; Sung-Joon Lee
abstract: Olfactory receptor 51E2 (OR51E2) is markedly downregulated in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet its functional activation by its natural agonist, β-ionone, suppresses CRC cell growth. In this study, we investigated the tumor-suppressive effects of β-ionone-mediated OR51E2 activation using human CRC cell lines (SW480, SW620, and RKO) and patient-derived organoids (PDOs). We demonstrate that β-ionone treatment stimulates intracellular calcium levels in an OR51E2-dependent manner, upregulating MAPK-directed phosphatases (DUSP1/2/4 and PPP1CA). This calcium-dependent phosphatase activation suppresses the MEK1/2-ERK1/2 signaling axis, leading to G0/G1 cell cycle arrest via the downregulation of CDK2/4/6 and cyclin A/D1. Concurrently, OR51E2 activation induces a senescence-like phenotype, evidenced by increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity, chromatin remodeling (reduced LAMIN B1 and increased H3K27me3), and upregulated p16/p21 expression alongside senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors. These phenotypic and mechanistic findings were fully recapitulated in CRC-PDOs representing distinct clinical subtypes. Crucially, the residual senescence-like cell population showed increased susceptibility to dasatinib plus quercetin (DQ), which reduced senescence-associated markers and increased apoptosis. Collectively, this study demonstrates that OR51E2 activation coordinates a heterogeneous cell-fate decision encompassing both apoptosis and a senescence-like phenotype. Our findings highlight ectopic olfactory receptor signaling as an underexplored mechanism of tumor suppression and provide in vitro evidence for a sequential approach in CRC in which β-ionone-mediated OR51E2 activation induces a senescence-like state followed by senolytic treatment.

title: Cellular senescence and vascular ageing in pulmonary hypertension: Molecular mechanisms, therapeutic strategies, and translational endpoints.
authors: Yide Chen; Xiaolan Wang; Meng Gao; Qinei Zheng; Qianyue Zhang; Ting Liu; Shuanglan Xu; Jiao Yang; Xiqian Xing
abstract: Increased right ventricular afterload, persistent pulmonary vascular remodelling, and the development of right heart failure are the hallmarks of pulmonary hypertension (PH). In PAH, therapies targeting the prostacyclin, nitric oxide-cyclic guanosine monophosphate, and endothelin pathways improve clinical status and haemodynamics, although established vascular remodelling frequently remains incompletely reversible. This review summarises data suggesting that the residual remodelling load in PH is influenced by vascular ageing, specifically stress-induced premature senescence-like phenotypes in pulmonary vascular wall cells. Endothelial repair failure, pulmonary artery smooth muscle cell secretory amplification, extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffening, senescence-associated secretory phenotype signalling, and mechano-metabolic reprogramming are examined as interconnected processes that attenuate vascular plasticity and consolidate disease progression. Pharmacological strategies discussed include senolytic and senomorphic approaches, activin/TGF-β superfamily modulation exemplified by sotatercept, matrix- and mechanotransduction-directed interventions, and metabolic modulation. Finally, vascular ageing-informed PH studies are proposed to incorporate concordant endpoints that align molecular target engagement with pulmonary vascular mechanics, right ventricular-pulmonary arterial (RV-PA) coupling, right ventricular function, and safety outcomes.

title: Cellular senescence in ageing and neurodegenerative disorders: Molecular mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies.
authors: Aanchal Verma; Ahsas Goyal; Neetu Agrawal; Harlokesh Narayan Yadav
abstract: Cellular senescence has been increasingly associated with neurodegenerative disorders, potentially linking ageing-related cellular impairment with mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and disrupted intercellular signalling. The present study aims to explore the increasing relevance of cellular senescence among key cell types, including neurons, astrocytes, neural progenitor cells, microglia and oligodendrocyte-lineage cells across neurodegenerative ailments such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and multiple sclerosis. This review discusses the findings of pre-clinical and clinical studies which suggest that senescence-associated features may contribute to neurodegeneration. Further, it provides an overview of the biomarkers used in the identification of senescence in the CNS. Also, the review examines senotherapeutic treatment approaches, highlighting their actions on different CNS cell types and the growing clinical evidence. It also points out the challenges in translating these approaches to clinical application, such as targeting specific cell types and the lack of suitable biomarkers. Collectively, present findings suggest that senescence-associated alterations may contribute to neurodegeneration, although their effects appear to vary across cell types and diseases.

title: Mapping cellular senescence in heart failure: Knowledge evolution, mechanistic modules, and senotherapeutic opportunities.
authors: Lichong Meng; Xiaoqian Liao; Zizheng Wu; Zhixi Hu
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cellular senescence is increasingly recognized as a mechanistic link between cardiovascular ageing, inflammatory-fibrotic remodelling, and heart failure (HF) progression. However, the knowledge structure, thematic evolution, and translational frontiers of senescence research in HF remain incompletely mapped. OBJECTIVE: This study mapped the global research landscape of cellular senescence in HF from 2005 to 2025 by integrating dual-database bibliometric analysis with BERTopic-based semantic topic modelling. METHODS: English-language articles and reviews were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus. After field verification, standardization, and deduplication, 479 publications were included. VOSviewer, CiteSpace, SCImago Graphica, Pajek, Python, and Microsoft Excel were used for bibliometric and visualization analyses. PubMedBERT-based embeddings and BERTopic were applied to identify latent semantic themes from titles, abstracts, and keywords. RESULTS: Publications increased rapidly after 2020, with 336 papers published between 2020 and 2025, accounting for 70.15% of the corpus. China and the United States were the leading contributors, with the United States showing higher collaboration strength and accumulated citation counts within the analysed dataset. Co-citation analysis identified foundational studies in senescence biology, senolytics, cardiovascular ageing, and HF remodelling. Keyword evolution showed a shift from oxidative stress, cardiac stem/progenitor cell senescence, and vascular cell senescence toward inflammation, metabolic remodelling, biomarkers, HF phenotypes, and senotherapeutics. BERTopic identified 17 substantive topics, with Cardiac and Cardiovascular Aging as the largest theme, followed by Cardiac Fibrosis and Fibroblast Activation, SASP-related Cardiovascular Senescence, Cardiac Regeneration, and Doxorubicin Cardiotoxicity. CONCLUSION: Bibliometric and semantic analyses indicate growing research interest in cell-type-specific senescence, inflammatory-fibrotic remodelling, HF phenotype heterogeneity, biomarkers, and senotherapeutics. These findings highlight opportunities for integrating mechanistic research with clinical investigation. Future studies should prioritize cell-specific senescence atlases, multidimensional biomarkers, comorbidity-aware HF stratification, and cautious evaluation of senotherapeutics in HF subgroups with evidence of senescence-associated pathology.

title: Death receptors regulate entry to therapy-induced senescence and orchestrate addiction to IAPs.
authors: Gokhan Gunay; Seren Hamsici; Vaishnavi Venugopalan; Aoife Costigan; Melanie Fritsch; Aislinn Gallagher Aldave; Anne Huber; Brianna Fernandez; Hande Efe-Cicek; Pavel Davidovich; Pavitha Parathan; Akash Srivaths; Natalie Hudson; Eleanor Noone; Jeffrey O'Callaghan; Lisa A Mielke; Sarah L Doyle; Sabrina L Spencer; Matthew Campbell; Conor J Kearney; Hamid Kashkar; Seamus J Martin
abstract: Cytotoxic chemotherapy typically results in the elimination of a fraction of the tumor with surviving cells entering a state of persistence or premature replicative senescence that can lead to recurrence. Here, we show that therapy-induced senescence is associated with robust up-regulation of Fas and/or TRAIL-R2/DR5 death receptors in vitro and in vivo. The latter receptors restricted entry to senescence and exerted selective pressure on senescent cells through promoting assembly of proapoptotic receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)/Fas-associated death domain protein (FADD)/Caspase-8 "FADDosome" complexes, restrained by cFLIPL. Accordingly, deletion of CASP-8 robustly enhanced entry to senescence and prolonged the life span of senescent cells. cIAP-2, which inhibits death receptor-driven cell death, was also up-regulated in senescent cells, and deletion of IAPs suppressed entry to senescence. Consistent with this, small-molecule IAP antagonists exhibited potent senolytic activity through enhancing death receptor-initiated Caspase-8 activation. Thus, death receptor-driven assembly of RIPK1/FADD/Caspase-8 complexes in senescent cells orchestrates addiction to IAPs that can be exploited by IAP antagonists.

title: Cellular Senescence as a Core Mechanistic Link between CKD, Cardiac Fibrosis, and Aging.
authors: Samuele Di Carmine; David P Baird; Katie J Mylonas
abstract: CKD and cardiovascular disease frequently coexist and represent a major global health burden. Cellular senescence may connect these disorders through persistent inflammation, fibrosis, and metabolic stress. Senescent cells undergo sustained proliferative arrest and release a pro-inflammatory, pro-fibrotic secretome called the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. In kidney and heart tissue, persistent senescent cells may promote immune-cell infiltration, fibroblast activation, extracellular matrix deposition, and tissue stiffening. Human biopsy, cardiac-tissue, urinary-biomarker, circulating-proteomic, and early senolytic data support associations between senescence markers, kidney dysfunction, and cardiovascular remodelling. However, most causal and interventional evidence still comes from cell-culture and animal models. This review critically evaluates cellular senescence as a plausible cardiorenal-fibrosis mechanism while emphasizing that causality, biomarker specificity, and therapeutic benefit in humans remain to be fully elucidated.

title: Immunosenescence and bone remodeling: from immune cell senescence to skeletal aging through the bone marrow microenvironment.
authors: Jinliang Zhuang; Weiwei Yu
abstract: With advancing age, the immune system undergoes progressive remodeling termed immunosenescence, which is intimately linked to skeletal homeostasis through the shared bone marrow microenvironment. This review systematically examines how senescent innate and adaptive immune cells disrupt bone remodeling by altering the cytokine milieu and releasing senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors. Aged macrophages exhibit enhanced M1 proinflammatory polarization, while neutrophils display increased oxidative burst and delayed apoptosis. Natural killer cells lose cytotoxic capacity, and dendritic cells show impaired antigen presentation yet elevated basal inflammation. Within the adaptive compartment, T helper 17 (Th17) cells expand, regulatory T cells (Tregs) undergo functional decline and lineage instability, and B cells shift from osteoprotegerin (OPG) production toward receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand (RANKL) expression. These changes collectively elevate the RANKL/OPG ratio, promote osteoclastogenesis, and suppress osteoblast function. Systemic factors including estrogen deficiency and gut dysbiosis further amplify this immune-driven bone loss. Emerging therapeutic strategies range from conventional anti-resorptive agents to senolytics and immune modulators that restore marrow homeostasis. Understanding immunosenescence as an important contributor to skeletal aging provides a conceptual framework for immune-centered prevention and treatment of osteoporosis and fracture complications in the elderly, while recognizing that direct human causal evidence remains limited for several immune cell populations.

title: Immune microenvironment in rotator cuff healing: from macrophage dynamics to immunomodulatory regenerative therapies.
authors: Feng Li; Zhengdao Fu; Xinhai Zhang; Xiurong Ke; Xiang Gao
abstract: Rotator cuff repair is increasingly limited by biology rather than fixation alone: the repaired tendon commonly heals through fibrovascular scar rather than recreating the graded tendon-fibrocartilage-bone enthesis, particularly in aging, metabolic disease, muscle degeneration, and poor bone quality. The immune microenvironment is a dynamic determinant of whether injury progresses toward persistent inflammation and fibrosis or toward resolution and regeneration. This Review synthesizes immune regulation across the rotator cuff muscle-tendon-enthesis-bone unit, with emphasis on macrophage heterogeneity, efferocytosis, autophagy, immunometabolism, mechanosensing, and immune-stromal crosstalk. Human single-cell studies identify pro-fibrotic macrophage, senescent tenocyte, osteopontin/TGF-beta, and endothelial programs in rotator cuff scar, while mechanistic studies nominate resolution pathways as therapeutic targets. We critically evaluate cytokine/chemokine modulation, extracellular vesicles, senomorphic strategies, bioactive ions, ROS-responsive materials, nanoengineered interfaces, and rehabilitation-based immunomodulation. Across these approaches, the key translational requirements are causal mechanism, validation in chronic or aged disease models and human tissue, integration of structural and mechanical outcomes, arthroscopic deployability, manufacturing feasibility, and biomarker-guided patient selection. Together, these data support a shift from nonspecific anti-inflammatory augmentation toward mechanism-based, pro-resolution strategies for durable tendon-to-bone repair.

title: The triad of vascular ageing: Cellular senescence, inflammaging, and epigenetic remodelling in atherosclerosis.
authors: Siarhei A Dabravolski; Daria D Borodko; Stanislav A Antonov; Svetlana S Lukina; Andrey A Poletaev; Vasily N Sukhorukov
abstract: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease remains a leading global cause of the cardiovascular mortality burden, yet traditional lipid-centric models fail to explain the residual cardiovascular risk observed in older populations. This review, synthesising contemporary literature from 2020 onwards alongside foundational studies, explores the paradigm shift towards the 'geroscience hypothesis', positing that intrinsic biological ageing of the vascular wall is a potent amplifier and primary driver of atherogenesis acting in synergy with circulating lipids. We delineate a pathogenic triad: cellular senescence, systemic inflammaging, and epigenetic dysregulation. At the cellular level, mechanical and metabolic stressors force endothelial and vascular smooth muscle cells into a usually stable senescent state, triggering the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype. Immunologically, ASCVD in the elderly is driven by metabolically exhausted macrophages, the emergence of clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential, and cytotoxic memory T cells. Crucially, metabolic stressors such as hyperglycaemia induce long-lasting alterations to the chromatin landscape of haematopoietic stem cells, establishing 'trained immunity' and a persistent pro-inflammatory metabolic memory. These processes are deeply governed by an altered epigenetic landscape, including the loss of protective sirtuins and aberrant RNA methylation, which dynamically accelerate biological clocks like GrimAge. Clinically, vascular ageing trajectories are highly sexually dimorphic and heavily influenced by midlife metabolic clustering and endocrine shifts and murine models suggest highly sexually dimorphic plaque immunophenotypes. Finally, we evaluate the translational frontier of precision senotherapeutics. We contrast senomorphics, such as repurposed metformin and natural polyphenols that suppress the SASP, with targeted senolytics. Emerging nanotechnology-including in vivo CAR-T lipid nanoparticles and responsive peptide nanoassemblies-offers preclinical proof-of-concept strategies to selectively clear senescent cells without systemic toxicity. Ultimately, mitigating ASCVD requires moving beyond lipid management to integratively target the biological clock of the artery.

title: Targeting Vascular Smooth Muscle Cell Senescence for Cardiovascular Pharmacology: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Perspectives.
authors: Alex El Darzi; Roy El Darzi; Karim Kanbar; Rabah Iratni; Hisham A Nematalla; Ali H Dakroub; Ali H Eid
abstract: Vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) play a central role in maintaining vascular tone, structural integrity, and adaptive remodeling. With aging and chronic cardiometabolic stress, however, VSMCs undergo senescence driven by telomere attrition, oxidative stress, persistent DNA-damage signaling, and dysregulation of the p53/p21 and p16/Rb pathways. This transition is accompanied by acquisition of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which promotes inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, calcification and vascular stiffening. Together, these accelerate atherosclerosis, hypertension, aneurysm formation, and related vasculopathies. Growing evidence identifies VSMC senescence as a promising therapeutic entry point for cardiovascular drug discovery. Emerging strategies include senolytics, senomorphics, metabolic modulators, and molecular reprogramming approaches designed to either eliminate senescent cells or attenuate their pathogenic secretome and downstream signaling networks. In this review, the molecular basis of VSMC senescence, its contribution to major vascular disorders, and the therapeutic landscape targeting senescence-associated pathways are discussed, with emphasis on translational opportunities and current barriers to clinical application. A clearer understanding of VSMC senescence may inform the development of mechanism-based interventions to limit vascular dysfunction and age-related cardiovascular disease.

title: Translating Geroscience Into Clinical Practice: Molecular Targets, Emerging Therapies, and Lifestyle Strategies for Healthy Longevity.
authors: Venkata BharatKumar Pinnelli; Surendra Babu T; Jayashankar C A; Harsha Anie Mathew; Venkataramana Kandi; Manish G R; Koshy T Sam; Atul S Sucharitha; Divyadharshini M S; Satya Vijaya Chandana Batchu; Rakshith C
abstract: Population aging has intensified interest in interventions that preserve function and delay multiple chronic diseases by modifying the biology of aging. The field now spans molecular geroscience, experimental therapeutics, biomarker development, and preventive medicine, but the maturity of evidence varies substantially. This study aimed to synthesize foundational mechanisms, clinical and translational strategies, and lifestyle determinants relevant to healthy longevity, while distinguishing established practice from emerging or unproven interventions. A critical narrative review of PubMed/MEDLINE and reference lists was conducted from January 2000 through August 2026. Priority was given to consensus frameworks, human randomized trials, prospective cohorts, systematic reviews, and influential mechanistic studies. Evidence was interpreted according to study design, clinical relevance, reproducibility, and safety. The expanded 12-hallmark framework depicts aging as an interconnected network involving genomic damage, impaired maintenance systems, maladaptive stress responses, inflammation, and dysbiosis. Senolytics, epigenetic reprogramming, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) augmentation, mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibition, metformin, and spermidine are biologically plausible, but none yet has definitive evidence of extending lifespan in healthy humans. Epigenetic clocks are useful research biomarkers, although a lower clock estimate is not synonymous with rejuvenation or proven risk reduction. By contrast, cardiorespiratory fitness, muscle strength, dietary quality, restorative and regular sleep, avoidance of tobacco, management of cardiometabolic risk, and social connection are supported by much stronger human-outcome evidence. Responsible longevity medicine should integrate geroscience with rigorous preventive care, use biomarkers as adjuncts rather than diagnoses, and reserve experimental geroprotectors for well-designed trials. The near-term opportunity is not radical life extension, but compression of morbidity through scalable, equitable, and evidence-based preservation of health span.

title: Cellular senescence is an early feature and therapeutic target in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis TDP-43Q331K mice.
authors: Jose A Viteri; Nathan R Kerr; Charles D Brennan; Grace R Kick; Meifang Wang; Arsh Ketabforoush; Harper J Snyder; Peter J Moore; Fereshteh B Darvishi; Anna R Dashtmian; Sindhuja N Ayyagari; Kelly Rich; Yi Zhu; Hiroshi Nishimune; W David Arnold
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive motor neuron degeneration in the motor cortex and spinal cord. Aging is a key risk factor for ALS, and cellular senescence - a hallmark of aging marked by irreversible cell-cycle arrest and a pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype - has been implicated in neurodegeneration, yet its role in ALS progression remains incompletely understood. Here, we show that molecular markers of cellular senescence emerge in the motor cortex and spinal cord alongside declines in neural and neuromuscular function in TDP-43Q331K ALS mice, supporting senescence as an early feature of ALS pathology. To test whether reduced senescence ameliorates ALS pathology, we evaluated longitudinal senolytic treatment with dasatinib and quercetin (D&Q) in TDP-43Q331K mice. D&Q treatment improved motor behavior, neuromuscular function, and reduced axonal damage as measured by plasma neurofilament light chain, accompanied by robust improvements in motor cortex excitability and preservation of layer V neuron counts. At the cellular level, cortical microglia were implicated as a potential mediator of senolytic benefits based on reduced microglial TDP-43 burden and senescence markers. Together, these findings identify cellular senescence as an early, disease-relevant, and modifiable feature of ALS pathology.

title: Advances in the study of the role of bone immunity in physiological and pathological processes related to bone metabolism.
authors: Zhuoru Jin; Lisheng Liu; Heran Wang; Yufei Wei; Zimo Zhou; Xiaohui Luo; Da Liu
abstract: BACKGROUND: Bone metabolism is regulated by immune cells that maintain skeletal homeostasis through cytokine secretion and cell interactions. Disruption of this regulation-by inflammation, autoimmunity, or aging-drives pathological bone diseases including osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis. Single-cell technologies and exosome biology have revealed previously unrecognized immune subsets and regulatory layers within the bone microenvironment. MAIN BODY: Osteoimmunology has elucidated the interplay between macrophages, T cells, B cells, NK cells, neutrophils, dendritic cells, and mast cells in bone remodeling. These cells form dynamic interaction networks-Treg-M2 feedback loops, Th17-neutrophil amplification, and B-T-osteoclast axes-that collectively determine net skeletal outcome. Immune cells regulate osteoclast and osteoblast function through TNF-α, IL-6, IL-17 A, and RANKL, with highly context-dependent effects. Immunosenescence has emerged as a key driver of age-related bone loss. The RANKL/RANK/OPG axis serves as the central signaling hub, modulated by Sema3A/Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, JAK/STAT, and Notch. Dysregulation of these pathways underlies osteoporosis, RA, intervertebral disc degeneration, ankylosing spondylitis, and cancer bone metastasis. Clinically, denosumab and cytokine-targeted biologics (anti-TNF-α, anti-IL-6R, anti-IL-17 A) demonstrate bone-protective effects, while bispecific antibodies, CAR-Treg cells, and senolytics represent emerging strategies. CONCLUSIONS: The net skeletal effect of the immune system is determined by the balance of interacting cell types, cytokine networks, and signaling pathways. Future progress requires single-cell spatiotemporal multi-omics, cell-type-specific immunotherapies, elucidation of the gut-bone axis, and systematic evaluation of combination strategies pairing immunomodulators with anti-resorptives, anabolic agents, or senolytics.

title: Silencing without clearing: pharmacological modulation of the SASP in aging and disease.
authors: Lukas Fresser; Zofia Chrienova; Jan Gebrt; Patrik Oleksak; Kamil Kuca; Eugenie Nepovimova
abstract: The global rise in life expectancy has led to an increasing prevalence of age-related diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders, cancer, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and cardiovascular conditions, placing substantial societal and economic burdens on healthcare systems worldwide. A key mechanism underlying both aging and these pathologies is cellular senescence (CS), now recognized as one of the 12 hallmarks of aging. Senescent cells exert their effects largely through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), a complex pro-inflammatory secretome that disrupts tissue homeostasis in neighbouring cells and actively promotes disease progression. This review first describes the biology of CS and the SASP in the context of aging and age-related pathologies, with emphasis on key regulatory pathways. We then provide a comprehensive overview of current senomorphic agents, i.e., compounds that modulate the SASP without eliminating senescent cells, covering their mechanisms of action, the signaling pathways they target, and the translational challenges they face. A particular focus is placed on the context-dependent dual role of the SASP. While its proinflammatory components drive tissue damage in chronic disease, SASP factors also contribute to wound healing, immune surveillance, and embryonic development. This duality has important implications for therapeutic design. Although senomorphics hold genuine promise as anti-aging interventions, substantial gaps remain between preclinical observations and clinical applicability. Future research must clarify the functions of individual SASP components, identify robust senescence biomarkers, and develop selective compounds with defined dose-response relationships and acceptable safety profiles.

title: Tumor-associated immunosenescence: Mechanisms, biomarkers and age-adaptive immunotherapy.
authors: Hongjiao Wu; Zhenbang Yang; Hongmei Zhang; Ye Jin; Shanshan Ji; Zhi Zhang; Guogui Sun; Xuemei Zhang
abstract: Immunosenescence alters immune-cell composition, signaling, metabolism, and regenerative capacity, but chronological age alone does not reliably predict response to cancer immunotherapy. In older adults, thymic involution, hematopoietic remodeling, inflammaging, and the accumulation of dysfunctional lymphoid and myeloid populations interact with tumor-derived suppressive signals. We organize these processes within an Immunosenescence-Immunotherapy Interference Axis linking systemic immune aging, local tumor remodeling, and treatment-specific vulnerabilities. Evidence is reviewed for senescence-like and exhausted CD8 + T cells, NK-cell dysfunction, age-associated macrophage states, loss of T-cell receptor diversity, and their relationship to immune checkpoint blockade. We then assess blood, tissue, and single-cell biomarkers that may distinguish biological immune age from chronological age, with particular attention to the limitations of single-marker classification. Finally, we critically evaluate senolytics, cytokine support, co-stimulatory approaches, and metabolic modulation as potential adjuncts to immunotherapy. The available evidence supports biomarker-informed, age-adaptive trial design, but prospective validation is required before immune-rejuvenation strategies can be recommended in routine oncology.

title: Cellular senescence in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
authors: Jilu Wang; Rui Liu; Xi Zhang; Guangwei Qi; Qiang Xu; Fuyun Jia
abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) contributes to nearly 50% of the global heart failure (HF) cases, and remains a major clinical challenge because of its heterogeneous pathophysiology, substantial residual morbidity, and limited mechanism-based treatment options. HFpEF is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous multisystem syndrome closely associated with aging, cardiometabolic comorbidities, and chronic low-grade inflammation. Cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) have emerged as potential mechanisms linking several of these systemic stressors to cardiovascular dysfunction. By paracrine and endocrine communication, SASP creates a self-reinforcing circuit in the myocardium. However, the biological consequences of cellular senescence are highly context-, cell type-, and stage-dependent, and transient senescence may exert adaptive or tissue-protective effects under certain conditions. Moreover, much of the current evidence linking senescence to HFpEF remains preclinical or associative, and HFpEF-specific human data are still limited. This review systematically assesses the current evidence linking cellular senescence and SASP to HFpEF and examines the therapeutic potential and limitations of senolytics and senomorphics.

title: Multidimensional Regulatory Network of Cellular Senescence: From Mechanisms to Theranostics.
authors: Zexiang Lv; Yanfei Liu; Yongbo Liu; Yifu Tan; Yunqi Man; Shuqing Du; Zhirou Zhang; Luke P Lee; Qi-Wen Chen; Zhenbao Liu
abstract: Cellular senescence is orchestrated by a complex and multidimensional regulatory network, whose functional outputs shift dynamically with disease stage and tissue context. This review systematically maps the molecular architecture of this network. The network encompasses the p53/p21 and p16/RB axes, mitochondrial stress pathways, and the cGAS-STING and mTOR-driven SASP programs. In parallel, the review traces how these mechanisms are rewired across a spectrum of pathological contexts, including cancer, metabolic and skeletal disorders, and organ-specific degenerative diseases. Building on this mechanistic foundation, we highlight theranostic innovations that integrate detection with intervention. These include enzyme-activatable prodrugs and probes that exploit senescence-associated markers such as SA-β-gal, enabling simultaneous imaging and cell clearance. Other examples are smart nanocarriers, which achieve spatiotemporally controlled drug delivery, and engineered immune cells, which restore immunosurveillance against senescent cells. Additionally, we discuss emerging platforms for dynamic quantification of senescent burden in vivo, including molecular imaging probes and liquid biopsy signatures. Despite promising preclinical progress, clinical translation remains limited by senescent-cell heterogeneity, off-target toxicity, and the lack of standardized biomarkers. By integrating mechanistic insights with theranostic design principles, this review provides a framework for developing precision strategies to detect, modulate, or eliminate senescent cells in a context-appropriate manner.

title: Cellular Senescence in Ocular Surface Diseases: Molecular Mechanisms and Therapeutic Perspectives.
authors: Linkang Zhang; Shipeng Li; Qiao Gao; Hongkun Zhang; Hong Zhang; Shudan Wang
abstract: Cellular senescence is characterized by stable cell-cycle arrest and a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Recurrent desiccating, oxidative, ultraviolet, microbial, and immune-mediated insults may induce stress-induced premature senescence (SIPS) in ocular surface tissues. PubMed and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 30 June 2026. Primary human, animal, and in vitro studies were prioritized, and direct evidence of senescence was distinguished from indirect stress-related or SASP-like associations. The p53-p21CIP1-pRB and p16INK4a-pRB pathways mediate senescence-associated cell-cycle arrest. Reactive oxygen species (ROS)-p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK) and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) signaling act as stress-sensing and inflammatory pathways, whereas mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) and AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) contribute to SASP and metabolic regulation. Transient senescence may support wound repair and immune clearance, whereas persistent senescence may contribute to epithelial and endothelial dysfunction, tear-film instability, immune dysregulation, fibrosis, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Mechanistic support is strongest in selected experimental models; evidence in several human ocular surface disorders remains associative. Cellular senescence is a context-dependent contributor to ocular surface pathology. Senolytic and senomorphic strategies remain predominantly preclinical and require disease-, cell-, and stage-specific validation.

title: Senescence-Associated Transcriptome Reversal Prioritizes Repurposing Candidates for Diabetic Kidney Disease: A Computational Study.
authors: Duygu Aygüneş-Jafari; Zekeriya Düzgün
abstract: Background/Objectives: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a leading cause of end-stage kidney disease, and cellular senescence is a tractable therapeutic target; yet prioritizing credible repurposing candidates is difficult because bulk-tissue senescence signals are weak, single-dataset analyses are unstable, and transcriptome-reversal screens overstate novelty. The objective was to build a senescence-anchored, multi-evidence computational prioritization of repurposing candidates for DKD entirely from open data. Methods: Per-sample senescence activity was quantified by single-sample gene set enrichment across three DKD kidney cohorts, and consensus signatures were reversed against 45,956 LINCS L1000 signatures. Candidates were ranked by reversal strength, mechanism, ChEMBL stage, and ClinicalTrials.gov novelty, then assessed for robustness by senotherapeutic enrichment, an external senolytic benchmark, leave-one-cohort-out analysis, drug-target Mendelian randomization, and single-nucleus profiling. Results: Senescence activity was consistently elevated in DKD across all three cohorts, with moderate-to-large effect sizes (rank-biserial 0.32-0.78). Reversal recovered established senotherapeutic classes and nominated the approved JAK inhibitor fedratinib (within the same class, baricitinib reduced albuminuria in a Phase 2 DKD trial); curated senolytics were modestly separated from negatives (AUROC 0.62, 95% CI 0.52-0.72). Filtering yielded 867 mechanism-annotated compounds robust to cohort removal. Drug-target Mendelian randomization was inconclusive, and single-nucleus profiling highlighted endothelial activation rather than a stable senescent compartment. Conclusions: The result is an externally benchmarked, novelty-annotated senotherapeutic candidate map, offered as convergent confirmation of repurposable mechanisms rather than a claim of new drug classes.

title: Decoding the immune regulation of ovarian aging: mechanisms and therapeutic strategies.
authors: Changjing Wang; Nianyu Li; Zi-Jiang Chen; Yingying Qin; Xue Jiao
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ovarian aging is among the earliest functional declines in humans and acts as a pacemaker of female aging. It encompasses both physiological age-related ovarian decline and pathological accelerated aging, exemplified by premature ovarian insufficiency (POI). Increasing evidence positions the immune system as both a regulator of ovarian homeostasis and a driver of ovarian dysfunction. Age-related immunosenescence and chronic low-grade inflammation (inflammaging) coordinately drive ovarian aging through bidirectional crosstalk between systemic immunity and the ovarian immune microenvironment. POI frequently coexists with autoimmune disorders, reinforcing the central role of the immune-ovarian axis in reproductive aging. Elucidating this interplay may enable targeted immunomodulatory strategies to preserve reproductive longevity and mitigate systemic consequences of ovarian decline. OBJECTIVE AND RATIONALE: The aim was to synthesize current evidence on (i) immune regulation of normal ovarian physiology; (ii) immune alterations in physiological ovarian aging, including systemic immunosenescence and ovarian immune microenvironment remodelling; (iii) autoimmune dysregulation in POI; and (iv) the translational potential of immunomodulatory interventions for mitigating ovarian aging. SEARCH METHODS: Original articles published up to April 2026 were identified through PubMed using combinations of the terms 'immune system', 'ovarian function', 'inflammation', 'immune cell', 'ovarian aging', 'menopause', 'primary ovarian insufficiency', and 'therapeutics'. OUTCOMES: Immune cells and cytokine networks form a specialized regulatory axis that governs folliculogenesis, ovulation, and luteal dynamics. This review synthesizes emerging evidence showing that this immune-ovary axis undergoes profound remodelling during reproductive aging and that immune dysregulation is a causal driver of ovarian functional decline. Systemically, the menopausal transition accelerates immunosenescence and amplifies pro-inflammatory cytokine production. Locally, the aging ovary exhibits chronic inflammation, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and accumulation of senescent cells with a senescence‑associated secretory phenotype. These changes coincide with a shift from tissue‑resident to monocyte‑derived macrophages and expansion of inflammatory γδ and double‑negative T cells. This progressive loss of immune homeostasis promotes follicular depletion, stromal fibrosis, and impaired steroidogenesis. POI represents a pathological extreme of this axis, characterized by autoimmune comorbidities, B cell-driven humoural abnormalities, T cell dysregulation, and genetic variants affecting immune pathways. Comparative analysis reveals both conserved inflammatory signatures shared with physiological aging and POI-specific immune features that reflect overt immune-mediated ovarian injury. By integrating systemic, local, and disease-specific immune mechanisms, this review reframes ovarian aging as a modifiable immunological process. Therapeutically, emerging immunomodulatory strategies range from molecular agents targeting inflammatory mediators and senescence programs, through cell-based immune reprogramming with stem cells, regulatory T cells, and senolytic immune effectors, to lifestyle-driven systemic immunomodulation. These strategies show promise in restoring ovarian immune homeostasis and extending the reproductive lifespan, with several of these approaches now advancing toward early-phase clinical evaluation. WIDER IMPLICATIONS: Collectively, the current evidence positions immune dysregulation as a mechanistic driver, rather than a secondary correlate, of ovarian aging. Integrating immune biomarkers into predictive frameworks and designing stratified immunomodulatory trials may shift ovarian aging management from symptomatic hormone replacement toward mechanism-based intervention. Reframing ovarian aging as a modifiable immune-mediated process offers new opportunities to extend female reproductive longevity and the female health span. REGISTRATION NUMBER: N/A.

title: Cellular senescence in ovarian cancer: a proposed geroncogenic shift linking aging, plasticity, and therapy resistance.
authors: Yubo Zhang; Yufei Han; Ping Hou; Weina Zhang; Meng Wu; Mengqi Deng
abstract: Ovarian cancer develops within a biological environment that changes substantially with age. Beyond chronological aging, progressive alterations in genome maintenance, telomere integrity, epigenetic regulation, mitochondrial function, metabolism, inflammation, and immune surveillance can reshape the cellular and tissue context in which tumor evolution occurs. Cellular senescence represents a critical point of convergence within this process. Although senescence can restrict the proliferation of damaged or oncogenically stressed cells, persistent senescent cells remain metabolically active and can alter their surroundings through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Here, we propose the concept of a geroncogenic shift to describe how age-associated changes in tissue homeostasis may create stress-response states that are subsequently exploited by malignant and stromal cells. We distinguish two named, complementary components of the framework: systemic decline, referring to the progressive deterioration of cellular and tissue homeostasis during aging, and pathway-specific hijacking, referring to the selective co-option of altered stress-response pathways under oncogenic or therapeutic pressure. Cellular senescence provides a functional interface between these processes because the same stress responses that constrain damaged cells can, when persistent or incompletely resolved, contribute to tumor adaptation. In ovarian cancer, senescence is not a uniform cellular endpoint. Its consequences vary according to the initiating stress, cellular compartment, molecular program, duration, and capacity for recovery or escape. Tumor-cell senescence may suppress proliferation yet also be associated with stem-like adaptation and therapeutic persistence. Senescence-associated changes in fibroblasts and other stromal populations can reshape inflammatory signaling and treatment response, while polyploid and senescence-like states illustrate the extent of cellular plasticity that can exist after therapeutic stress. The SASP further extends the effects of senescence beyond individual cells by influencing neighboring tumor and stromal populations, extracellular-matrix remodeling, inflammation, and dissemination. This perspective has important therapeutic implications. Rather than treating senescence as either a uniformly protective or pathogenic state, therapeutic strategies should distinguish between senescent-cell elimination, SASP modulation, metabolic vulnerabilities, and prevention of senescence escape. We propose that understanding the cellular context and temporal dynamics of senescence will be essential for determining when senescence should be induced, maintained, modulated, or eliminated in ovarian cancer. Most therapeutic evidence for senescence-directed strategies remains preclinical, and clinical translation will require cell-type-specific biomarkers and optimized treatment timing. The geroncogenic shift framework therefore provides a conceptual basis for linking aging biology with tumor evolution and for developing more selective approaches to senescence-directed therapy.

title: Biomarker-Guided, Stage-Specific Senotherapy for Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease.
authors: Yunhang Chu; Wenqi Jin; Weigeng She; Qi Meng; Liwei Sun; Yan Leng
abstract: Cellular senescence drives inflammation and fibrosis progression in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Existing research covers hepatocyte types, SASP signaling pathways, and senescence-targeting drugs. However, basic mechanistic understanding and precise clinical translation remain disconnected. An integrative therapeutic framework that couples senescence heterogeneity with disease stage-specific microenvironmental contexts is still lacking. This Perspective presents a hypothesis-generating translational framework and a candidate sequential trial design. The proposed sequence would combine short-term senescent cell clearance with long-term senescence modulation and metabolic maintenance. By stratifying senescence biomarkers according to clinical decision functions into patient selection markers, treatment timing markers, and response efficacy markers, and by defining candidate therapeutic windows based on disease stages, this study proposes lifestyle intervention and senescence modulation as proposed preventive strategies during simple steatosis, the testing of short-term senescent cell clearance during metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and fibrosis within prospective trial settings, and careful evaluation of intervention feasibility and anticipated benefits under strict risk stratification during cirrhosis. Patients with active hepatocellular carcinoma or high-risk premalignant lesions should currently be excluded from early senolytic trials pending dedicated safety data, rather than being described as an absolute clinical contraindication. This work aims to provide an actionable and verifiable reference framework for precise translation of senescence-targeted therapy in MASLD, moving the field from whether it works toward for whom it works, when it works, and how to test it safely and effectively. All proposed thresholds, strategies, and sequences are candidate endpoints for prospective validation.

title: Organoids for modeling cellular senescence and age-related pathology: From experimental reconstruction to mechanistic and translational applications.
authors: Zhonglu Yang; Huifang Sun; Fan Zhang; Wei Ji; Youde Liang; Min Wang; Mingdong Yan; Zifan Zhao; Liangliang Fu
abstract: Cellular senescence, characterized by irreversible cell cycle arrest and the acquisition of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), is a fundamental hallmark of aging and a key driver of numerous age-related diseases. However, conventional two-dimensional cell cultures and animal models fail to fully replicate the complex cellular architecture, multicellular interactions, and tissue-specific microenvironments in which senescence develops in vivo. Organoids, three-dimensional tissue models derived from pluripotent or adult stem cells, have emerged as physiologically relevant platforms that recapitulate selected aspects of human tissue organization, cellular diversity, and functional characteristics. These features make organoids well suited for investigating the mechanisms, dynamics, and pathological consequences of cellular senescence. In this review, we summarize recent advances in organoid-based models for senescence research, highlighting their physiological relevance, strategies for organoid generation, approaches for inducing and characterizing senescence, and their applications in modeling age-related diseases. We further discuss the emerging roles of organoids in senescence-targeted drug discovery, regenerative medicine, and precision therapeutics. While organoids provide experimentally tractable platforms for dissecting the biology of cellular senescence and accelerating the development of therapeutic strategies for aging and age-related diseases, their capacity to fully recapitulate the complexity of human aging remains limited. Future advances in vascularization, immune integration, multi-organ systems, spatial multi-omics, and artificial intelligence-assisted analyses may help address these limitations and further enhance the physiological relevance and translational potential of organoid-based models.

title: Cellular senescence in multiple sclerosis: hallmarks, immunosenescence, and therapeutic implications.
authors: Ala' Yousef; John M Seubert; Christopher Power; Nabeela Nathoo
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated neurodegenerative disease where chronological aging predicts the conversion to progressive MS (PMS), a phase defined by compartmentalized inflammation and accelerated neurodegeneration. While current disease modifying therapies (DMTs) are effective for managing the inflammatory aspect of MS, treatments remain inadequate. It is imperative to understand the biology of aging including an important hallmark of aging, cellular senescence. Cellular senescence is a state of cell cycle arrest where cells remain in their senescent state and produce a distinctive senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), characterized by the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors. Growing experimental and clinical evidence suggests that the accumulation of senescent cells and SASP secretion perpetuates a pathological feedback loop linking age-related processes with accelerated neurodegeneration observed in PMS. Whether senescence drives PMS or accompanies it remains unresolved. In this Review, we outline the biology of aging, senescence pathway markers, and SASP components. We evaluate studies of cellular senescence and SASP markers in MS, including immunosenescence, T- and B-cell changes; the contributions of Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus-1; and the relationship between senescence burden, brain atrophy, and DMT response. Lastly, we outline the available senotherapeutic approaches aimed at mitigating MS and other neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Nanoparticle-based senolytic and senomorphic therapies for healthy aging: design principles, translational evidence, and challenges.
authors: Jiaqing Huang; Lichen Ji; Huihui Jin; Zhike Shi; Xiaolu Song; Yu Cai; Xiangmin Tong
abstract: Cellular senescence contributes to age-associated tissue dysfunction through persistent growth arrest, metabolic remodeling, and altered communication with immune and stromal cells. Senolytic therapies preferentially eliminate susceptible senescent cells, while senomorphic therapies modulate harmful senescence-associated activities. Nanoparticle engineering can improve the delivery of these agents through cargo protection, surface functionalization, and controlled release. Surface ligands can promote cellular uptake, and components responsive to lysosomal β-galactosidase, acidic pH, reactive oxygen species, or protease activity can regulate cargo release. The selectivity of these mechanisms depends on biological features that vary among senescent populations and also occur in other cellular states. This review examines how material composition and physicochemical properties influence target recognition, intracellular transport, therapeutic activity, and safety. Representative platforms are evaluated across fibrotic, musculoskeletal, metabolic, oncologic, and neurodegenerative disease models, with particular attention to mitochondrial delivery, immune-mediated clearance, nucleic-acid modulation, and microbiome interactions. Preclinical findings are considered alongside human senotherapy studies, which have primarily evaluated small-molecule drug regimens and yielded preliminary or mixed outcomes. Clinical development requires reproducible manufacturing, pharmacokinetic characterization of both carrier and cargo, and assessment of immunotoxicity and delayed organ injury in older hosts. Progress depends on matching a defined pathological cell population to an appropriate delivery strategy and demonstrating an advantage in therapeutic index or sustained functional outcomes against relevant comparators, including clinically feasible non-nanoparticle treatments where available.

title: Is there a role for senotherapeutics in the treatment of giant cell arteritis?
authors: Chiara Marvisi; Nicolò Pipitone; Claudio Franceschi; Stefania Croci; Carlo Salvarani
abstract: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is a large-vessel vasculitis predominantly affecting individuals over 50 years, with a peak incidence between 70 and 80 years. Its pathogenesis involves complex immunological cascades triggered by vascular dendritic cell activation, recruitment of CD4⁺ T cells and monocytes, T helper lymphocyte polarization, and vascular remodeling driven by myofibroblasts and fibroblasts. Growing evidence implicates cellular senescence (particularly in vascular smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and immune cells) in the pathophysiology of GCA. Senescent cells (SC) accumulate in affected arteries and display a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), producing pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and matrix metalloproteinases, thereby perpetuating inflammation and tissue injury. Senotherapeutics (agents targeting SC) are broadly classified into senolytics, which induce SC apoptosis, and senomorphics, which suppress SASP without eliminating SC. Candidate senolytics include fisetin, quercetin, curcumin, and dasatinib, which also show anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and vascular-protective effects, although some may cause adverse vascular consequences. Senomorphics such as resveratrol, kaempferol, apigenin, epigallocatechin gallate, rapamycin, metformin, and ruxolitinib modulate NF‑κB, mTOR, JAK/STAT, and sirtuin pathways, potentially reducing vascular inflammation, restoring immune balance, and preventing remodeling, besides acting on aging-associated modifications. As current treatments primarily suppress inflammation and may not fully target age-related mechanisms contributing to persistent vascular injury, investigating cellular senescence as a potentially actionable component of GCA biology is timely. Key challenges include selecting optimal agents, timing, dosing, and duration, while avoiding adverse vascular effects. The aim of this review was to identify potential clinical and translational applications of senotherapeutic compounds for GCA to guide future research in this field.

title: Senotherapeutic potential against xeroderma pigmentosum.
authors: Xuebing Wang; Masako Nishida; Ai Yoshioka; Claire Yik-Lok Chung; Shinya Hashimoto; Hideki Tanizawa; Shinya Ohta; Ken-Ichi Noma; Takeshi Fukumoto
abstract: BACKGROUND: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an inherited photoaging syndrome caused by mutations in genes involved in the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway. XP patients exhibit hypersensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) radiation, leading to accelerated skin aging and requiring lifelong sun avoidance. In this study, we aimed to investigate UV-induced cellular senescence in XP melanocytes and explore potential senotherapeutic strategies. METHODS: Melanocytes differentiated from iPSCs derived from an XP-A patient and a healthy individual, respectively, were used to induce senescence. Senescence was assessed by SA-β-gal and γH2AX staining. The drug screening tested a panel of 12 senolytic agents and 15 senomorphic agents for their ability to target senescent XP-iMCs. The effects of these agents were evaluated through cell viability assays and SPiDER-βGal staining followed by flow cytometry. RNA sequencing was performed to analyze transcriptional changes induced by senomorphic treatments. RESULTS: We demonstrate that UV-induced DNA damage triggers cellular senescence and up-regulates senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) genes in melanocytes derived from an XP patient. The drug screening identified JAK inhibitors and curcuminoids as promising senomorphic agents. In addition, two classes of senolytic agents, BCL-2-like protein inhibitors and HSP90 inhibitors, effectively eliminate senescent melanocytes. Further analysis demonstrates that senomorphic treatment effectively counteracts senescence and reduces SASP gene expression in XP-derived melanocytes. Moreover, genes in senescence-related pathways, including the cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, JAK/STAT, and PI3K/AKT pathways, which are activated in senescent cells, are down-regulated by senomorphic treatment. CONCLUSIONS: This study highlights a potential senotherapeutic strategy for XP, which may help alleviate photoaging symptoms in XP patients.

title: Therapeutic reversal of cellular senescence: A systematic review of senolytics, senomorphics and anti-ageing therapies in human clinical trials.
authors: Hitesha Trivedi; Suraj Tripathi; Jalay Thacker; Nilesh Patil; Sohel Shaikh
abstract: Cellular senescence, a key feature of ageing, involves irreversible cell cycle arrest and the secretion of pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors, which contribute to tissue degeneration and age-related diseases. Targeting senescent cells with senolytics, senomorphics and anti-ageing therapies marks a major shift in translational geroscience, with the potential to delay or reverse age-related conditions. A systematic review and narrative synthesis was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Eligible human clinical studies evaluating pharmacological interventions targeting cellular senescence were included, comprising randomized and nonrandomized clinical trials and pilot studies reporting clinical, functional or senescence-associated outcomes. Data on study characteristics, interventions, efficacy, safety and senescence-associated biomarkers were extracted and synthesized qualitatively. Six completed clinical studies were included in the evidence synthesis, with one additional ongoing clinical trial identified separately. Senolytic interventions, particularly dasatinib plus quercetin, showed preliminary improvements in selected functional outcomes and reductions in senescence-associated biomarkers, while senomorphic and mTOR-targeting interventions demonstrated effects on selected tissue and immune-related outcomes. Reported adverse events were generally mild or manageable, but small sample sizes and short follow-up limited assessment of uncommon and long-term safety risks. Current evidence suggests that pharmacological targeting of cellular senescence is feasible and may produce measurable biological and functional effects in humans, but evidence remains insufficient to establish clinical efficacy or long-term safety. Senolytic and senomorphic strategies should therefore be considered investigational rather than established therapies. Larger, adequately powered randomized trials with standardized senescence biomarkers, clinically meaningful outcomes, longer follow-up and systematic safety assessment are needed.

title: The Molecular Landscape of the Senescence-EMT Interplay: Deciphering Tumour Plasticity Through Molecular Signatures and Multi-Omic Profiling.
authors: Eva M Verdugo-Sivianes; Carmen Campos-Silva; José Luis García-Márquez; Elena Aguado-Domínguez
abstract: Therapy-induced senescence (TIS) is a common response to anticancer treatments, characterised by stable cell cycle arrest and the acquisition of a complex senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Initially regarded as a beneficial mechanism that limits tumour growth, growing evidence indicates that TIS is a highly dynamic and heterogeneous process with context-dependent effects that can either suppress or promote tumour progression. The SASP is a central mediator of tumour plasticity, linking TIS to epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), cancer stemness, microenvironmental remodelling, therapeutic resistance, and metastatic dissemination. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of senotherapeutic approaches, including senolytic and senomorphic agents, as key components of one-two-punch therapeutic strategies to selectively eliminate or modulate persistent senescent cells and improve treatment outcomes. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies, artificial intelligence, and liquid biopsy are further transforming the study of senescence by enabling comprehensive molecular characterisation, biomarker discovery, patient stratification, and real-time monitoring of tumour evolution. Collectively, current evidence supports a paradigm shift in which senescence should be considered a dynamic regulator of tumour plasticity and a promising target for precision oncology strategies.

title: Ginkgolide B as a Candidate Gerotherapeutic: Evidence, Evidentiary Limits, and Translational Requirements.
authors: Joanna Y Yang; Doris T Tu; Yun-Lin Chen; Oscar K Lee
abstract: Aging is a systemic process in which redox imbalance, cellular senescence, progenitor-cell dysfunction and chronic inflammation converge on frailty and functional decline, and geroscience seeks compounds that modulate several at once. What is more often missing is an explicit standard for deciding when a compound qualifies as a candidate gerotherapeutic.
